5-manifold is a [5-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5-dimensional) [topological manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_manifold), possibly with a [piecewise linear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piecewise_linear_structure) or [smooth structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_structure).

Aeppli cohomology is a [cohomology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_theory) for [complex manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold).

AF+BG theorem (also known as Max Noether's fundamental theorem) is a result of [Max Noether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Noether) that asserts that, if the equation of an [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) in the [complex projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_projective_plane) belongs locally (at each intersection point) to the [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) generated by the equations of two other algebraic curves, then it belongs globally to this ideal.

Special affine curvature, also known as the equiaffine curvature or affine curvature, is a particular type of [curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature) that is defined on a plane [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve) that remains unchanged under a [special affine transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_affine_group) (an [affine transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_transformation) that preserves [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area)).

Alexandrov spaces with curvature ≥ k form a generalization of [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold)s with [sectional curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature_of_Riemannian_manifolds) ≥ k, where k is some real number.

Alexandrov's soap bubble theorem is a mathematical theorem from [geometric analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_analysis) that characterizes a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) through the [mean curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_curvature).

algebraic cycle on an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) V is a formal linear combination of [subvarieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subvariety_(algebraic_geometry)) of V.

Algebraic geometry is a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) which uses [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra)ic techniques, mainly from [commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra), to solve [geometrical problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry).
algebraic geometry and analytic geometry are two closely related subjects.

Algebraic K-theory is a subject area in mathematics with connections to [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry), [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology), [ring theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_theory), and [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory).

Alla Sheffer is a Canadian researcher in [computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_graphics), [geometric modeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_modeling), [geometry processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry_processing), and [mesh generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesh_generation), particularly known for her research on [mesh parameterization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesh_parameterization) and angle-based flattening.

almost-contact structure is a certain kind of geometric structure on a [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold), obtained by combining a [contact-element structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_structure) (not necessarily a contact structure) and an [almost-complex structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost-complex_structure).

ambient space is the space surrounding a [mathematical object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_object) along with the object itself.

amenable group is a [locally compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_compact) [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group) G carrying a kind of averaging operation on [bounded function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_function)s that is [invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_(mathematics)) under translation by group elements.
amplituhedron is a geometric structure introduced in 2013 by [Nima Arkani-Hamed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nima_Arkani-Hamed) and Jaroslav Trnka.

Anabelian geometry is a theory in [arithmetic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_geometry) which describes the way in which the [algebraic fundamental group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_fundamental_group) of a certain [arithmetic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_variety) X, or some related geometric object, can help to recover X.

analyst's traveling salesman problem is an analog of the [traveling salesman problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traveling_salesman_problem) in [combinatorial optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial_optimization).

analytic geometry, also known as coordinate geometry or Cartesian geometry, is the study of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) using a [coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_system).

Reidemeister torsion (or R-torsion, or Reidemeister–Franz torsion) is a [topological invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_invariant) of [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s introduced by [Kurt Reidemeister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Reidemeister) for [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold)s and generalized to higher [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)s by and .

Anderson's theorem is a result in [real analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_analysis) and [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) which says that the [integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral) of an integrable, symmetric, unimodal, non-negative function f over an n-dimensional [convex body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_body) K does not decrease if K is translated inwards towards the origin.
André planes are a class of finite [translation plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_plane)s found by André.

André–Oort conjecture is a problem in [Diophantine geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_geometry), a branch of [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory), that can be seen as a non-abelian analogue of the [[Arithmetic of abelian varieties#Manin–Mumford conjecture|Manin–Mumford conjecture]], which is now a theorem (proven in several different ways).

Angenent torus is a smooth [embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embedding) of the [torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torus) into three-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space), with the property that it remains self-similar as it evolves under the [mean curvature flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_curvature_flow).

angular defect or simply defect (also called deficit or deficiency) is the failure of some [angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle)s to add up to the expected amount of 360° or 180°, when such angles in the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane) would.

angular diameter, angular width, angular size, apparent diameter, or apparent size is an [angular separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_separation) (in [units of angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Units_of_angle)) describing how large a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) or [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle) appears from a given point of view.
Anisotropy () is the structural property of non-uniformity in different directions, as opposed to [isotropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotropy).
Anisotropic energy is energy that is directionally specific.
annulus theorem (formerly called the annulus conjecture) states roughly that the region between two well-behaved spheres is an [annulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annulus_(mathematics)).

Anosov map on a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) M is a certain type of mapping, from M to itself, with rather clearly marked local directions of are called [horocycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horocycle)s.

anthropomorphic polygon is a [simple polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_polygon) with precisely two [ear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ear_(mathematics))s and one [mouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mouth_(mathematics)).

antimatroid is a [formal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_system) that describes processes in which a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) is built up by including elements one at a time, and in which an element, once available for inclusion, remains available until it is included.

antipodal or diametrically opposite if they are the endpoints of a [diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diameter), a straight [line segment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_segment) between two points on a sphere and passing through its [center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_(geometry)).
apeirotope or infinite polytope is a generalized [polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope) which has infinitely many [facets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facet_(geometry)).

Apollonian circles are two families ([pencils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pencil_(geometry))) of [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle)s such that every circle in the first family intersects every circle in the second family [orthogonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal)ly, and vice versa.

Apollonian gasket, Apollonian net, or Apollonian circle packing is a [fractal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal) generated by starting with a triple of circles, each tangent to the other two, and successively filling in more circles, each [tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent) to another three.
Apollonian network is an [undirected graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undirected_graph) formed by a process of recursively subdividing a triangle into three smaller triangles.
Apollonian sphere packing is the three-dimensional equivalent of the [Apollonian gasket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollonian_gasket).

apotome is a line segment formed from a longer line segment by breaking it into two parts, one of which is [commensurable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commensurability_(mathematics)) only in power to the whole; the other part is the apotome.

Appell–Humbert theorem describes the [line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_bundle)s on a [complex torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_torus) or complex [abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety).

approximation theorems are an extension of the [Chinese remainder theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_remainder_theorem) to [algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_group)s G over [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field)s k.

Arakelov theory (or Arakelov geometry) is an approach to [Diophantine geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_geometry), named for [Suren Arakelov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suren_Arakelov).

bivariant theory was introduced by [Fulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Fulton_(mathematician)) and [MacPherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_MacPherson_(mathematician)) , in order to put a ring structure on the [Chow group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group) of a [singular variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_variety), the resulting ring called an [operational Chow ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_Chow_ring).
Björling problem is the problem of finding a [minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface) passing through a given curve with prescribed normal (or tangent planes).

Blaschke selection theorem is a result in [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) and [convex geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_geometry) about [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence)s of [convex set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set)s.

Bloch sphere is a geometrical representation of the [pure state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_state) space of a [two-level quantum mechanical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-level_system) ([qubit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qubit)), named after the physicist [Felix Bloch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Bloch).

Bloch's higher Chow groups, a generalization of [Chow group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_group), is a precursor and a basic example of [motivic cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivic_cohomology) (for smooth varieties).
blocking set is a set of points in a [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane) that every line intersects and that does not contain an entire line.
Bochner's formula is a statement relating [harmonic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_functions) on a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) .

Bombieri–Lang conjecture is an unsolved problem [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture)d by [Enrico Bombieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Bombieri) and [Serge Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serge_Lang) about the [Zariski density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zariski_topology) of the set of [rational point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_point)s of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) of [[Kodaira dimension#General type|general type]].

bond length or bond distance is defined as the average distance between [nuclei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_nucleus) of two [bonded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_bond) [atom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom)s in a [molecule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecule).

Bonnesen's inequality is an [inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inequality_(mathematics)) relating the length, the area, the radius of the [incircle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incircle) and the radius of the [circumcircle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumcircle) of a [Jordan curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_curve).

Boolean operations on polygons are a set of [Boolean operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_operation_(Boolean_algebra))s (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, ...) operating on one or more sets of [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon)s in computer graphics.

Borel fixed-point theorem is a [fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed-point_theorem) in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) generalizing the [Lie–Kolchin theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie–Kolchin_theorem).

Borel's theorem, due to , says the [cohomology ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_ring) of a [classifying space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classifying_space) or a [classifying stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classifying_stack) is a [polynomial ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_ring).

Borell–Brascamp–Lieb inequality is an [integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral) [inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inequality_(mathematics)) due to many different mathematicians but named after [Christer Borell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christer_Borell), [Herm Jan Brascamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herm_Jan_Brascamp) and [Elliott Lieb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott_Lieb).
Bott–Chern cohomology is a [cohomology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_theory) for [complex manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold).
Bott–Samelson resolution of a [Schubert variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_variety) is a [resolution of singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_of_singularities).

bounding interval hierarchy (BIH) is a partitioning [data structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure) similar to that of [bounding volume hierarchies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounding_volume_hierarchy) or [kd-tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kd-tree)s.

bounding volume (or bounding region) for a set of objects is a [closed region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_region) that completely [contains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Containment_(set_theory)) the [union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(mathematics)) of the objects in the set.
bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) is a [tree structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_structure) on a set of [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric) objects.

Boy's surface is an [immersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immersion_(mathematics)) of the [real projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_projective_plane) in [three-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space).

bracket ring is the [subring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subring) of the [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) of [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s k[x indexed by the λ.
Brahmagupta triangle is a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) whose side lengths are consecutive positive integers and area is a positive integer.
branched surface is a generalization of both [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(topology))s and [train track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_track_(mathematics))s.
Brascamp–Lieb inequality is either of two inequalities.

Brauer group of a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K is an [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group) whose elements are [Morita equivalence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morita_equivalence) [classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_class) of [central simple algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_simple_algebra)s over K, with addition given by the [tensor product of algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product_of_algebras).

Brianchon's theorem is a theorem stating that when a [hexagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexagon) is [circumscribed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumscribed) around a [conic section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conic_section), its principal [diagonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonal)s (those connecting opposite vertices) meet in a single point.
Bride's Chair is an illustration of the [Pythagorean theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_theorem).
Bridgeland stability condition is an algebro-geometric stability condition defined on elements of a [triangulated category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulated_category).

Brieskorn–Grothendieck resolution is a resolution conjectured by [Alexander Grothendieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grothendieck), that in particular gives a resolution of the universal deformation of a [Kleinian singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kleinian_singularity).

British flag theorem says that if a point P is chosen inside a [rectangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangle) ABCD then the sum of the [squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_(algebra)) of the [Euclidean distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance)s from P to two opposite corners of the rectangle equals the sum to the other two opposite corners.

Brittany Terese Fasy is an American computer scientist and applied mathematician specializing in [computational topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_topology), [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry), and [topological data analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_data_analysis).

definition: Brunn–Minkowski theorem (or Brunn–Minkowski inequality) is an inequality relating the volumes (or more generally [Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_measure)s) of [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset)s of [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space).

Bryant surface is a 2-dimensional surface embedded in 3-dimensional [hyperbolic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_space) with constant [mean curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_curvature) equal to 1.

Buchberger's algorithm is a method for transforming a given set of polynomials into a [Gröbner basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gröbner_basis), which is another set of polynomials that have the same common zeros and are more convenient for extracting information on these common zeros.
Budan's theorem is a theorem for bounding the number of real roots of a polynomial in an interval, and computing the [parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)) of this number.

Buekenhout geometry or diagram geometry is a generalization of [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space)s, [Tits building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tits_building)s, and several other geometric structures, introduced by .

buffer analysis is the determination of a [zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locus_(mathematics)) around a [geographic feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_feature) containing locations that are within a specified distance of that feature, the buffer zone (or just buffer).
Buffon's needle problem is a question first posed in the 18th century by [Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges-Louis_Leclerc,_Comte_de_Buffon): (1937).

Buffon's noodle is a variation on the well-known problem of [Buffon's needle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffon's_needle), named after [Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges-Louis_Leclerc,_Comte_de_Buffon) who lived in the 18th century.

building (also Tits building, named after [Jacques Tits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Tits)) is a combinatorial and geometric structure which simultaneously generalizes certain aspects of [flag manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_manifold)s, finite [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane)s, and [Riemannian symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_symmetric_space)s.

bundle gerbe is a [geometrical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) model of certain 1-[gerbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerbe)s with [connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_(mathematics)), or equivalently of a 2-class in [Deligne cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deligne_cohomology).

definition: Burt's solar compass or astronomical compass/sun compass is a [surveying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveying) instrument that makes use of the Sun's direction instead of magnetism.

Busemann functions are used to study the large-scale geometry of geodesics in [Hadamard space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_space)s and in particular [Hadamard manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_manifold)s ([simply connected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simply_connected) complete [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold)s of nonpositive curvature).

Busemann's theorem is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) in [Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry) and [geometric tomography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_tomography).

Busemann–Petty problem, introduced by , asks whether it is true that a symmetric [convex body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_body) with larger central [hyperplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperplane) sections has larger volume.

C.a.R. (Compass and Ruler), also known as Z.u.L. (), is a free and open source [interactive geometry app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interactive_geometry_software) that can do geometrical constructions in [Euclidean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry) and [non-Euclidean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Euclidean) [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry).

definition: Calabi conjecture was a conjecture about the existence of certain kinds of [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric)s on certain [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold)s, made by .

Calabi flow is a [geometric flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_flow) which deforms a [Kähler metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kähler_metric) on a [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold).

calibrated manifold is a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) (M,g) of dimension n equipped with a [differential p-form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form) 262}}.

Camera auto-calibration is the process of determining internal [camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinhole_camera_model) parameters directly from multiple uncalibrated images of unstructured scenes.

Camera resectioning is the process of estimating the parameters of a [pinhole camera model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinhole_camera_model) approximating the camera that produced a given photograph or video; it determines which incoming [light ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_ray) is associated with each pixel on the resulting image.

Canberra distance is a numerical measure of the distance between pairs of points in a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space), introduced in 1966 [[Category:Digital geometry]] [[Category:Metric geometry]] [[Category:Distance]] bnnmu3pa1fnpt1nr5coqdk3deh523q3

Cannon–Thurston map is any of a number of continuous group-equivariant maps between the boundaries of two [hyperbolic metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_metric_space)s extending a discrete isometric actions of the group on those spaces.

canonical coordinates are sets of [coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinates) on [phase space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_space) which can be used to describe a physical system at any given point in time.

pluricanonical ring of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) V (which is [[Algebraic curve#Singularities|nonsingular]]), or of a [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold), is the [graded ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graded_commutative_ring) : , called the n-canonical map.

canonical singularities are a class of singularities that appear on the [[Canonical_bundle#Canonical_rings|canonical model]] of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety), and terminal singularities are a narrower class that occur as singularities of [minimal models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_model_program).

cant of a [railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport) track or [camber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camber_angle) of a road (also referred to as superelevation, [cross slope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_slope), cross fall, or difference in crosslevel) is the difference in elevation (height) between the two rails or edges of the road.

cant deficiency is defined in the context of travel of a [rail vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport) at constant speed on a constant-radius [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve).

Carathéodory conjecture is a mathematical [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) attributed to [Constantin Carathéodory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_Carathéodory) by [Hans Ludwig Hamburger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Ludwig_Hamburger) in a session of the Berlin Mathematical Society in 1924.

Carathéodory metric is a [metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_(mathematics)) defined on the [open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set) [unit ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_ball) of a [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) [Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space) that has many similar properties to the [Poincaré metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincaré_metric) of [hyperbolic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_geometry).
Carathéodory's theorem is a theorem in [convex geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_geometry).

[Carathéodory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_Carathéodory)–[Jacobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Gustav_Jakob_Jacobi)–[Lie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophus_Lie) theorem is a theorem in [symplectic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_geometry) which generalizes [Darboux's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darboux's_theorem).

cardinal directions or cardinal points are the four main [compass directions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_directions): [north](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North) (N), [east](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East) (E), [south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South) (S), and [west](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West) (W).

cardinal points consist of three pairs of [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) located on the [optical axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_axis) of a [rotationally symmetric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_symmetry), focal, optical system.

Carlyle circle is a certain [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle) in a [coordinate plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_plane) associated with a [quadratic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_equation); it is named after [Thomas Carlyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carlyle).
CaRMetal is an [interactive geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_interactive_geometry_software) program which inherited the [C.a.R.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C.a.R.) engine.

carpenter's rule problem is a [discrete geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_geometry) problem, which can be stated in the following manner: Can a [simple planar polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_polygon) be moved continuously to a position where all its vertices are in [convex position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_position), so that the edge lengths and simplicity are preserved along the way? A closely related problem is to show that any non-self-crossing [polygonal chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygonal_chain) can be straightened, again by a continuous transformation that preserves edge distances and avoids crossings.
Cartan connection is a flexible generalization of the notion of an [affine connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_connection).

Cartan's equivalence method is a technique in [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry) for determining whether two geometrical structures are the same up to a [diffeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffeomorphism).

Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks theorem is a theorem of [Riemannian geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_geometry), according to which the [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric) is locally determined by the [Riemann curvature tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_curvature_tensor), or in other words, behavior of the curvature tensor under parallel translation determines the metric.

Cartan–Hadamard conjecture is a fundamental problem in [Riemannian geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_geometry) and [geometric measure theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_measure_theory) which states that the classical [isoperimetric inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isoperimetric_inequality) may be generalized to spaces of nonpositive [sectional curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sectional_curvature), known as [Cartan–Hadamard manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_manifold).

Cartan–Hadamard theorem is a statement in [Riemannian geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_geometry) concerning the structure of complete [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold)s of non-positive [sectional curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sectional_curvature).
Cartan–Karlhede algorithm is a procedure for completely classifying and comparing [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold)s.

Cartesian coordinate system (, ) in a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) is a [coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_system) that specifies each [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) uniquely by a pair of [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)s called coordinates, which are the [signed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_and_negative_numbers) distances to the point from two fixed [perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular) [oriented line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriented_line)s, called [coordinate line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_line)s, coordinate axes or just axes (plural of axis) of the system.

Cartier isomorphism is a certain [isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism) between the [cohomology sheaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_of_sheaves) of the [de Rham complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_de_Rham_cohomology) of a [smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_scheme) [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) of [positive characteristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_characteristic), and the sheaves of [differential form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form)s on the [[Frobenius endomorphism#Frobenius for schemes|Frobenius twist]] of the variety.

Casey's theorem, also known as the generalized [Ptolemy's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy's_theorem), is a theorem in [Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry) named after the Irish [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) [John Casey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Casey_(mathematician)).
Casson handle is a 4-dimensional topological [2-handle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handle_(mathematics)) constructed by an infinite procedure.

Casson invariant is an integer-valued invariant of oriented integral [homology 3-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_3-sphere)s, introduced by [Andrew Casson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Casson).
Castelnuovo's contraction theorem is also called an [exceptional curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exceptional_curve) of the first kind.
Castelnuovo–de Franchis theorem is a classical result on complex [algebraic surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_surface)s.

Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity of a [coherent sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf) F over [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) is finitely generated and has the same regularity as F.

CAT(0) group is a [finitely generated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group) [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) with a [group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) on a [CAT(0) space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAT(0)_space) that is geometrically proper, [cocompact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocompact_group_action), and [isometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry).

Catalan surface, named after the Belgian [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) [Eugène Charles Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugène_Charles_Catalan), is a [ruled surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruled_surface) all of whose generators are parallel to a fixed [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)).

Catalan's minimal surface is a [minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface) originally studied by [Eugène Charles Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugène_Charles_Catalan) in 1855.

Catalogue of Triangle Cubics is an online resource containing detailed information about more than 1200 [cubic curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_plane_curve) in the plane of a reference triangle.

categorical quotient of an object X with [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) G is a [morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphism) Kirwan, F.
categorical trace is a generalization of the [trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_(linear_algebra)) of a [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)).

Met is a [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) that has [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space)s as its [objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_(category_theory)) and [metric map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_map)s ([[Continuous_function#Continuous_functions_between_metric_spaces|continuous]] [functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) between metric spaces that do not increase any pairwise distance) as its [morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphism)s.
[Affine geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_geometry) is the [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) of affine space of a given dimension n over a field K.

coordinate system is a system for assigning an n-[tuple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuple) of [number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number)s or [scalars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_(mathematics)) to each [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) in an n-[dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)al space.

[Discrete geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_geometry) or combinatorial geometry may be loosely defined as study of geometrical objects and properties that are [discrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_mathematics) or [combinatorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial), either by their nature or by their representation; the study that does not essentially rely on the notion of [continuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function).
Euclidean solid geometry is the traditional [solid geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_geometry) of [three-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space).

Fractals are [self-similar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-similarity) geometric objects with both [aesthetical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesthetics) and [scientific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science) uses.
General relativity is the best known relativistic [classical field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_field_theory) of [gravitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitation).
Geometric graph theory is a branch of [graph theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_theory).
geometric group theory is the study of groups by geometric methods.

Geometry in computer vision is a sub-field within [computer vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_vision) dealing with geometric relations between the 3D world and its projection into 2D image, typically by means of a [pinhole camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinhole_camera_model).

Moduli theory is a branch of the fields of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry), [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold)s and [singularity theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_theory).

[polyform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyform) is a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)) figure constructed by joining together identical basic [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon)s.

quaternions are a non-commutative extension of the [complex number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number)s which have numerous applications in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics), and [computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_graphics).
Riemannian geometry is the study of [smooth manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) with [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric)s; i.e.
Symplectic geometry is a part of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) which studies [symplectic manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_manifold)s.
[tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor) is a certain kind of geometrical entity and [array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) concept.
topology is a branch of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) concerned with the study of [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space)s.
[triangle center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle_center) is a point constructed from a triangle in a way that is independent of the triangle's placement and scale.

Trigonometry (from the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language) trigonon = three angles and metro = measure) is a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) dealing with [angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle)s, [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle_(geometry))s and [trigonometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_function)s such as [sine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine), [cosine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosine) and [tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent).

[variable-sweep wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable-sweep_wing) (swing-wing) is a type of pivoted [wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wing) that takes advantage of the aerodynamics of a [swept wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swept_wing) at high speeds while swinging straight to avoiding the drawbacks of such a design at lower speeds.

catenary ( , ) is the [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve) that an idealized hanging [chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain) or [cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wire_rope) assumes under its own [weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weight) when supported only at its ends in a uniform [gravitational field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_field).
Cauchy's theorem is a theorem in [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry), named after [Augustin Cauchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustin-Louis_Cauchy).

caustic is the [envelope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(mathematics)) of [[Line (mathematics)#Ray|ray]]s either [reflected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflection_(mathematics)) or [refracted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refracted) by a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold).

Cayley–Klein metric is a [metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_(mathematics)) on the [complement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complement_(set_theory)) of a fixed [quadric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadric) in a [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) which is defined using a [cross-ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-ratio).

CC system or counterclockwise system is a [ternary relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_relation) introduced by [Donald Knuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Knuth) to model the clockwise ordering of triples of points in [general position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_position) in the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane).

cellular decomposition G of a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) M is a decomposition of M as the disjoint union of cells (spaces [homeomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism) to n-balls B .

center of balance of a [horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse) is a position on the horse's [back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_(horse)) which correlates closely to the [center of gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_gravity) of the horse itself.

center of curvature of a curve is a point located at a distance from the [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve_(mathematics)) equal to the [radius of curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius_of_curvature_(mathematics)) lying on the [curve normal vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve_normal_vector).

term: Center of gravity of an aircraft
page: Center of gravity of an aircraft
definition: center of gravity (CG) of an aircraft is the point over which the aircraft would balance.

center of mass of a distribution of [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass) in [space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space) (sometimes referred to as the barycenter or balance point) is the unique point at any given time where the weighted [relative position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Position_(geometry)) of the distributed mass sums to zero.

definition: center of percussion is the point on an extended massive object attached to a pivot where a [perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular) impact will produce no reactive shock at the pivot.

center of pressure is the point on a body where a single [force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force) acting at that point can represent the total effect of the [pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure) field acting on the body.
center of pressure (CoP) is the term given to the point of application of the [ground reaction force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_reaction_force) vector.

center-of-momentum frame (COM frame) of a system, also known as zero-momentum frame, is the [inertial frame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_frame) in which the total [momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum_(physics)) of the system vanishes.
centerpoint is a generalization of the [median](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median) to data in higher-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space).

term: Centers of gravity in non-uniform fields
page: Centers of gravity in non-uniform fields

definition: central angle is an [angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle) whose apex (vertex) is the center O of a circle and whose legs (sides) are [radii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius) intersecting the circle in two distinct points A and B.

centre ([Commonwealth English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_in_the_Commonwealth_of_Nations)) or center ([American English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English)) () of an [object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape) is a [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) in some sense in the middle of the object.

definition: centroid, also known as geometric center or center of figure, of a [plane figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_figure) or [solid figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_figure) is the [mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_mean_of_a_function) [position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Position_(geometry)) of all the points in the figure.

centroidal Voronoi tessellation (CVT) is a special type of [Voronoi tessellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voronoi_tessellation) in which the generating point of each Voronoi cell is also its [centroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centroid) (center of mass).

Century Gothic is a digital [sans-serif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sans-serif) typeface in the [[Sans-serif#Geometric|geometric]] style, released by [Monotype Imaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monotype_Imaging) in 1990.
Ceva's theorem is a theorem about [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle)s.
Chandrajit Bajaj (born 1958 in Calcutta, India) is an American [computer scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_scientist).

Cheeger isoperimetric constant of a [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) M is a positive real number h(M) defined in terms of the minimal [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_area) of a [hypersurface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersurface) that divides M into two disjoint pieces.

Chentsov's theorem states that the [Fisher information metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information_metric) is, up to rescaling, the unique [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric) on a [statistical manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_manifold) that is invariant under [sufficient statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufficient_statistics).

Chern's conjecture for affinely flat manifolds was proposed by [Shiing-Shen Chern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiing-Shen_Chern) in 1955 in the field of [affine geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_geometry).

term: Chern's conjecture for hypersurfaces in spheres
page: Chern's conjecture for hypersurfaces in spheres
definition: Chern's conjecture for hypersurfaces in spheres, unsolved as of 2018, is a [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) proposed by [Chern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiing-Shen_Chern) in the field of [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry).
Chern–Simons forms are certain secondary [characteristic class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_class)es.

Chern–Weil homomorphism is a basic construction in Chern–Weil theory that computes [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) invariants of [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle)s and [principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)s on a [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold) M in terms of [connections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_(mathematics)) and [curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature) representing classes in the [de Rham cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rham_cohomology) rings of M.

Chevalley–Iwahori–Nagata theorem states that if a [linear algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebraic_group) G is [acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) linearly on a finite-dimensional [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space) V, then the map from V/G to the [spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_ring) of the ring of [invariant polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_theory) is an [isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_isomorphism) if this ring is finitely generated and all [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) of G on V are [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_set) .

Chow groups (named after [Wei-Liang Chow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wei-Liang_Chow) by ) of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) over any [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) are algebro-geometric analogs of the [homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_(mathematics)) of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space).
Chow's lemma, named after [Wei-Liang Chow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wei-Liang_Chow), is one of the foundational results in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).

Chow's moving lemma, proved by , states: given [algebraic cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_cycles) Y, Z on a [nonsingular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_variety) [quasi-projective variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-projective_variety) X, there is another algebraic cycle Z' which is [rationally equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationally_equivalent) to Z on X, such that Y and Z' intersect properly.
Christoffel symbols are an array of numbers describing a [metric connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_connection).

Cinderella is a [proprietary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proprietary_software) [interactive geometry software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interactive_geometry_software), written in [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_programming_language).
circle graph is the [intersection graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_graph) of a [chord diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_diagram_(mathematics)).

circle of antisimilitude (also known as mid-circle) of two [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle)s, α and β, is a reference circle for which α and β are [inverses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversive_geometry) of each other.
circuit topology of a folded linear [polymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymer) is the arrangement of its intra-molecular contacts.

circular points at infinity (also called cyclic points or isotropic points) are two special [points at infinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_at_infinity) in the [complex projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_projective_plane) that are contained in the [complexification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complexification) of every real [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle).

circular section is a [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle) on a [quadric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadric) surface (such as an [ellipsoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipsoid) or [hyperboloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperboloid)).
circular-arc graph is the [intersection graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_graph) of a set of [arcs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_(geometry)) on the circle.
circumcevian triangle is a special [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) associated with a reference triangle and a point in the plane of the triangle.
circumference () is the [perimeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perimeter) of a [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle) or [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse).

circumgon is a geometric figure which [circumscribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumscribed_circle) some [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle), in the sense that it is the union of the outer edges of non-overlapping triangles each of which has a vertex at the center of the circle and opposite side on a line that is tangent to the circle.

circumscribed sphere of a [polyhedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyhedron) is a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) that contains the polyhedron and touches each of the polyhedron's [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)).
Cis–trans isomerism, also known as geometric isomerism, describes certain arrangements of atoms within molecules.

Clairaut's relation, named after [Alexis Claude de Clairaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Claude_de_Clairaut), is a formula that characterizes the great circle paths on the [unit sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_sphere).

clasper is a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(topology)) (with extra structure) in a [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold) on which [surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgery_theory) can be performed.

classical Wiener space is the collection of all [[Continuous_function#Continuous_functions_between_metric_spaces|continuous functions]] on a given [domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_of_a_function) (usually a [subinterval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subinterval) of the [real line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_line)), taking values in a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space) (usually n-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space)).
classification of manifolds is a basic question, about which much is known, and many open questions about [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s remain.

Clifford analysis, using [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra)s named after [William Kingdon Clifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kingdon_Clifford), is the study of [Dirac operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_operator)s, and Dirac type operators in analysis and geometry, together with their applications.

Clifford bundle is an [algebra bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_bundle) whose fibers have the structure of a [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra) and whose [local trivialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_trivialization)s respect the algebra structure.

Clifford module bundle, a bundle of Clifford modules or just Clifford module is a [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle) whose fibers are [Clifford module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_module)s, the representations of [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra)s.
Clifford parallel or paratactic lines if the [perpendicular distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular_distance) between them is constant from point to point.

Clifford's theorem on special divisors is a result of on [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve)s, showing the constraints on [special linear system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_linear_system)s on a curve C.

Clifton–Pohl torus is an example of a [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) [Lorentzian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentzian_manifold) that is not [geodesically complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesically_complete).

Clock angle problems are a type of [mathematical problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_problem) which involve finding the angle between the hands of an [analog clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_clock).

close-packing of equal spheres is a dense arrangement of congruent [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere)s in an infinite, regular arrangement (or [lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_(group))).

closed geodesic on a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) is a [geodesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic) that returns to its starting point with the same tangent direction.

closed manifold is a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) [without boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold_with_boundary) that is [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space).

closed point of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) is a [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) whose [singleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singleton_(mathematics)) is [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_set).

closing of a set ([binary image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_image)) A by a [structuring element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structuring_element) B is the [erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erosion_(morphology)) of the [dilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilation_(morphology)) of that set, : .
clutching construction is a way of constructing fiber bundles, particularly vector bundles on spheres.

coarse structure on a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) X is a collection of [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset)s of the [cartesian product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product) X × X with certain properties which allow the large-scale structure of [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space)s and [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space)s to be defined.

codimension is a basic [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) idea that applies to [subspaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_subspace) in [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)s, to [submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold)s in [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s, and suitable [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset)s of [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_varieties).

digital image is an [image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image) composed of [picture element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel)s, also known as [pixels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel), each with [finite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_number), [discrete quantities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_mathematics) of numeric representation for its [intensity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude) or [gray level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gray_level) that is an output from its [two-dimensional functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) fed as input by its [spatial coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spatial_coordinates) denoted with x, y on the x-axis and y-axis, respectively.

Digital modeling and fabrication is a design and production process that combines [3D modeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_modeling) or [computing-aided design (CAD)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-aided_design) with additive and subtractive [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing).

dihedral angle is the [angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle) between two [intersecting planes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane–plane_intersection) or [half-plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-plane)s.
Dilation (usually represented by ⊕) is one of the basic operations in [mathematical morphology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_morphology).

Ding-Zhu Du (born May 21, 1948) is a Professor in the Department of [Computer Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science) at [The University of Texas at Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_University_of_Texas_at_Dallas).

Diophantine geometry is the study of [Diophantine equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_equation)s (the search for integer solutions of polynomial equations) by means of powerful methods in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).

DiProDB is a [database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_structure_database) designed to collect and analyse [thermodynamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermodynamics), [structural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_structure) and other [dinucleotide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinucleotide) properties.

Dirac structure is a geometric structure generalizing both [symplectic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_structure)s and [Poisson structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_structure)s, and having several applications to mechanics.

direction, also known as spatial direction, vector direction or relative direction, is the common characteristic of all [rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_(geometry)) which coincide when [translated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_(geometry)) to share a common endpoint; equivalently, it is the common characteristic of [vectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_(geometry)) (such as the [relative position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_position) between a pair of points) which can be made equal by [scaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scaling_(geometry)) (by some positive [scalar multiplier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_multiplication)).

definition: direction cosines (or directional cosines) of a [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector) are the [cosine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosine)s of the angles between the vector and the three positive coordinate axes.
Discrete differential geometry is the study of discrete counterparts of notions in [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry).

Discrete geometry and combinatorial geometry are branches of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) that study [combinatorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics) properties and constructive methods of [discrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_mathematics) geometric objects.

discrete Laplace operator is an analog of the continuous [Laplace operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_operator), defined so that it has meaning on a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) or a [discrete grid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_(group)).

displacement is a [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector) whose length is the shortest [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance) from the initial to the final [position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Position_(vector)) of a point P undergoing [motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion).

dissection problem is the problem of partitioning a geometric [figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape) (such as a [polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope) or [ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_(mathematics))) into smaller pieces that may be rearranged into a new figure of equal content.

distance between two [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(graph_theory)) in a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) is the number of edges in a [shortest path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_path_problem) (also called a graph geodesic) connecting them.

[distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance) between two [parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_(geometry)) [lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)) in the [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) is the minimum distance between any two points.

term: Distance from a point to a line
page: Distance from a point to a line
definition: distance (or perpendicular distance) from a point to a line is the shortest [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance) from a fixed [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) to any point on a fixed infinite [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(mathematics)) in [Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry).

term: Distance from a point to a plane
page: Distance from a point to a plane
definition: distance from a point to a plane is the distance between a given point and its [orthogonal projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal_projection) on the plane, the [perpendicular distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular_distance) to the nearest point on the plane.
related: Distance from a point to a line

definition: Distance geometry is the branch of mathematics concerned with [characterizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characterization_(mathematics)) and studying [sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) of points based only on given values of the [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance)s between pairs of points.

distance matrix is a [square matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_matrix) (two-dimensional array) containing the [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance)s, taken pairwise, between the elements of a set.
distance set of a collection of points is the [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) of [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance)s between distinct pairs of points.
distance transform, also known as distance map or distance field, is a derived representation of a [digital image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_image).

distortion is a measure of the amount by which a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) from the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane) to itself distorts circles to ellipses.

term: Distribution on a linear algebraic group
page: Distribution on a linear algebraic group
definition: distribution on it is a linear functional .
divisors are a generalization of [codimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codimension)-1 subvarieties of [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_varieties).

divisorial scheme is a [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) admitting an ample family of line bundles, as opposed to an [ample line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ample_line_bundle).
dodecahedral conjecture in [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) is intimately related to [sphere packing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_packing).

Doignon's theorem in [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) is an analogue of [Helly's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helly's_theorem) for the [integer lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_lattice).

Donaldson theory is the study of the topology of smooth [4-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4-manifold)s using [moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space)s of [[Yang–Mills_equations#Anti-self-duality_equations|anti-self-dual instantons]].
Donaldson–Thomas theory is the theory of Donaldson–Thomas invariants.

dose-fractionation theorem for [tomographic imaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomographic_imaging) is a [statement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statement_(logic)) that says the total dose required to achieve [statistical significance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_significance) for each [voxel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voxel) of a computed [3D reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_reconstruction) is the same as that required to obtain a single [2D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_space) image of that isolated voxel at the same level of statistical significance.

double vector bundle is the combination of two compatible [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle) structures, which contains in particular the tangent is a double vector bundle.

double wedge is the ([closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closure_(topology)) of) the [symmetric difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_difference) of two [half-space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-space_(geometry))s whose boundaries are not parallel to each other.
downstream refers to data sent from a [network service provider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_service_provider) to a customer.

IsoAxis () is a geometric [net](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_(polyhedron)) consisting of sixty [isosceles triangles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isosceles_triangle) that, when scored and folded, forms a movable three-dimensional ring capable of continuous inversion.

perfect tiling is the [tessellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation) of a portion of the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane) in which all tiles are [similar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Similarity_(geometry)) to each other and to the entire portion, but no tile is [congruent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_(geometry)) with any other.

Drinfeld module (or elliptic module) is roughly a special kind of [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) over a ring of functions on a curve over a [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field), generalizing the Carlitz module.
Du Bois singularities are singularities of [complex varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_algebraic_variety) studied by Du Bois.

dual bundle is an operation on [vector bundles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle) extending the operation of [duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_vector_space) for [vector spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space).

dual curve of a given [plane curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_curve) is a curve in the [dual projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duality_(projective_geometry)) consisting of the set of lines [tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent) to .

duality or plane duality is a formalization of the striking [symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry) of the roles played by [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) and [lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)) in the definitions and theorems of [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane)s.

dualizing sheaf on a [proper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proper_scheme) [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) X of dimension n over a field k is a [coherent sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf) to construct the dualizing sheaf on X.

Dupin hypersurface is a [submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold) in a [space form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_form), whose [principal curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_curvature)s have globally constant multiplicities.
Dupin indicatrix is a method for characterising the local shape of a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(differential_geometry)).

Dwork family is a one-parameter family of [hypersurface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersurface)s depending on an integer n, studied by [Bernard Dwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Dwork).

Dykstra's algorithm is a method that computes a point in the intersection of [convex set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set)s, and is a variant of the [alternating projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternating_projection) method (also called the [projections onto convex sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projections_onto_convex_sets) method).

dévissage is a technique introduced by [Alexander Grothendieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grothendieck) for proving statements about [coherent sheaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf) on [Noetherian scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_scheme)s.

E-plane and H-plane are reference [planes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) for [linearly polarized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearly_polarized) [waveguide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waveguide_(electromagnetism))s, [antennas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antenna_(radio)) and other [microwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave) devices.
earthquake map is a method of changing one [hyperbolic manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_manifold) into another, introduced by .
East is one of the four [cardinal direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_direction)s or [points of the compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Points_of_the_compass).
eccentricity of a [[Conic section#Eccentricity|conic section]] is a non-negative real number that uniquely characterizes its shape.

ecliptic or ecliptic plane is the apparent path of the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun) on the [celestial sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_sphere), resulting from [Earth's orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_orbit) around the Sun.
