definition: edge is a particular type of [line segment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_segment) joining two [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)) in a [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon), [polyhedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyhedron), or higher-dimensional [polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope).

effective dimension is a modification of [Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension) and other [fractal dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal_dimension)s that places it in a [computability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computability_theory) setting.

Eguchi–Hanson space is a non-compact, [self-dual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-dual), asymptotically locally Euclidean (ALE) metric on the [cotangent bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotangent_bundle) of the 2-sphere T [[Category:Differential geometry]] [[Category:String theory]] oxg1ih6j1147xwlbacdfze1ai9w37a7
Egyptian geometry refers to [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) as it was developed and used in [Ancient Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt).

eight-point algorithm is an algorithm used in [computer vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_vision) to estimate the [essential matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_matrix) or the [fundamental matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_matrix_(computer_vision)) related to a [stereo camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_camera) pair from a set of corresponding image points.

Einstein notation (also known as the Einstein summation convention or Einstein summation notation) is a notational convention that implies [summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summation) over a set of indexed terms in a formula, thus achieving brevity.

Einstein–Weyl geometry is a smooth [conformal manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_manifold), together with a compatible [Weyl connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_connection) that satisfies an appropriate version of the [Einstein vacuum equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_equations), first considered by and named after [Albert Einstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein) and [Hermann Weyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Weyl).

Eisenstein triple (named after [Gotthold Eisenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gotthold_Eisenstein)) is a set of [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)s which are the lengths of the sides of a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) where one of the angles is 60 or 120 degrees.
eleven-point conic is a [conic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conic) associated to four points and a line, containing 11 special points.

elimination theory is the classical name for algorithmic approaches to eliminating some variables between [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s of several variables, in order to solve [systems of polynomial equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_of_polynomial_equations).
Elliptic geometry is an example of a [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) in which Euclid's [parallel postulate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_postulate) does not hold.

elliptic surface is a surface that has an elliptic [fibration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibration), in other words a [proper morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proper_morphism) with connected [fibers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_(mathematics)) to an [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) such that almost all fibers are [smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_scheme) curves of [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus_(mathematics)) 1.

ELSV formula, named after its four authors , , [Michael Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Shapiro_(mathematician)), [Alek Vainshtein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alek_Vainshtein), is an equality between a Hurwitz number (counting [ramified covering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramified_covering)s of the sphere) and an integral over the [moduli space of stable curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_of_algebraic_curves).

Enriques surfaces are [algebraic surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_surface)s such that the irregularity q = 0 and the [canonical line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_line_bundle) K is non-trivial but has trivial square.
Enriques–Babbage theorem states that a [canonical curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_curve) is either a set-theoretic intersection of quadrics, or trigonal, or a plane quintic.

enumerative geometry is the branch of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) concerned with counting numbers of solutions to geometric questions, mainly by means of [intersection theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_theory).

envelope of a planar [family of curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_of_curves) is a [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve) that is [tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent) to each member of the family at some point, and these points of tangency together form the whole envelope.

equal incircles theorem derives from a Japanese [Sangaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangaku), and pertains to the following construction: a series of rays are drawn from a given point to a given line such that the inscribed circles of the triangles formed by adjacent rays and the base line are equal.

Equant (or punctum aequans) is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical) concept developed by [Claudius Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudius_Ptolemy) in the 2nd century AD to account for the observed motion of the planets.

equiareal map, sometimes called an authalic map, is a [smooth map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_map) from one [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)) to another that preserves the [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area)s of figures.

equichordal point is a point defined relative to a [convex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set) plane curve such that all [chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_(geometry)) passing through the point are equal in length.

equichordal point problem is the question whether a [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_curve) [planar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) [convex body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_body) can have two [equichordal point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equichordal_point)s.
Equidimensional is an adjective applied to objects that have nearly the same size or spread in multiple directions.

equidissection is a [partition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_a_set) of a [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon) into [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle)s of equal [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area).

definition: equilateral dimension of a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space) is the maximum size of any subset of the space whose points are all at equal distances to each other.
equisingularity is, roughly, a family of singularities that are not non-equivalent and is an important notion in [singularity theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_theory).
equivalent latitude is a [Lagrangian coordinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_coordinates) .

equivariant differential form on a manifold M [acted upon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group_action) by a [Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group) G is a [polynomial map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_map) : -exact forms are called equivariantly closed or equivariantly exact.

equivariant index theorem, of which there are several variants, computes the (graded) trace of an element of a compact [Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group) acting in given setting in terms of the integral over the [fixed points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_point_(mathematics)) of the element.

Erdős–Diophantine graph is an object in the [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) subject of [Diophantine equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_equations) consisting of a set of [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) points at integer distances in the plane that cannot be extended by any additional points.

Erdős–Nagy theorem is a result in [discrete geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_geometry) stating that a non-convex [simple polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_polygon) can be made into a [convex polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polygon) by a finite sequence of flips.
Erdős–Szekeres theorem asserts that, given 1), so that either the first row is of length at least r or the last row is of length at least s.

Erdős–Ulam problem asks whether the plane contains a [dense set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dense_set) of points whose [Euclidean distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance)s are all [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number)s.

Erlangen program is a method of characterizing [geometries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) based on [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory) and [projective geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_geometry).

Erosion (usually represented by ⊖) is one of two fundamental operations (the other being [dilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilation_(morphology))) in [morphological image processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphological_image_processing) from which all other morphological operations are based.
essential manifold is a special type of closed manifold.

term: Estimation of signal parameters via rotational invariance techniques
page: Estimation of signal parameters via rotational invariance techniques
definition: Estimation of signal parameters via rotational invariant techniques (ESPRIT), is a technique to determine the parameters of a mixture of [sinusoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_wave)s in background noise.

Euclidean distance between two [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) in a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) is the [length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length) of the [line segment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_segment) between them.

Euclidean plane is a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) of [dimension two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_space), denoted Such a drawing is called a plane graph or planar embedding of the graph.

Euclidean plane isometry is an [isometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry) of the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane), or more informally, a way of transforming the plane that preserves geometrical properties such as length.
related: Rotations and reflections in two dimensions

definition: plane is a [flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_space) two-[dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)al [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(geometry)) that extends indefinitely.

Euclidean shortest path problem is a problem in [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry): given a set of [polyhedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyhedron) obstacles in a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space), and two points, find the shortest path between the points that does not intersect any of the obstacles.
Euclidean space is the fundamental space of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry), intended to represent [physical space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_space).

term: Euclidean tilings by convex regular polygons
page: Euclidean tilings by convex regular polygons

definition: Euler angles are three angles introduced by [Leonhard Euler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonhard_Euler) to describe the [orientation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientation_(geometry)) of a [rigid body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_body) with respect to a fixed [coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_system).

Euler brick, named after [Leonhard Euler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonhard_Euler), is a [rectangular cuboid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangular_cuboid) whose [edges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(geometry)) and [face diagonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_diagonal)s all have integer lengths.

Euler calculus is a methodology from applied [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology) and [integral geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_geometry) that integrates [constructible function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructible_function)s and more recently [definable function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definable_function)s 219.

Euler characteristic of an orbifold, or orbifold Euler characteristic, is a generalization of the [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) [Euler characteristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_characteristic) that includes contributions coming from nontrivial [automorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism)s.

Euler's formula, named after [Leonhard Euler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonhard_Euler), is a [mathematical formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_formula) in [complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis) that establishes the fundamental relationship between the [trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions) and the complex [exponential function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_function).
Euler's theorem is a result on the [curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature) of [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve)s on a surface.

Euler–Arnold equations are a class of [partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation)s (PDEs) that describe the [[Geodesic#Geodesic flow|geodesic flow]] on infinite-dimensional [Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group)s equipped with right-invariant [metrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_tensor).
event is anything that happens that has a specific time and place in [spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime).

quasi-excellent ring is a [Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) [commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring) that behaves well with respect to the operation of [completion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completion_of_a_ring), and is called an excellent ring if it is also [universally catenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_catenary).

expansion is a [polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope) operation where [facets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facet_(mathematics)) are separated and moved radially apart, and new facets are formed at separated elements ([vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)), [edges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(geometry)), etc.).

exsphere of a face of a regular polyhedron is the sphere outside the polyhedron which touches the face and the planes defined by extending the adjacent faces outwards.
Eyeball theorem: red chords are of equal length.
F-crystals are objects introduced by that capture some of the structure of [crystalline cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystalline_cohomology) groups.

face is a flat [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface) (a [planar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) [region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region_(mathematics))) that forms part of the boundary of a solid object.

face diagonal of a [polyhedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyhedron) is a [diagonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonal) on one of the [faces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faces_(geometry)), in contrast to a [space diagonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_diagonal) passing through the interior of the polyhedron.

Faithfully flat descent or flat descent is a technique from [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry), allowing one to draw conclusions about objects on the target of a [faithfully flat morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faithfully_flat_morphism).

fake 4-ball is a [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compactness_(topology)) [contractible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contractible_space) topological [4-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4-manifold).

fake projective space is a complex [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) that has the same [Betti number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betti_number)s as some [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space), but is not [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphic) to it.

Falconer's conjecture, named after [Kenneth Falconer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Falconer_(mathematician)), is an [unsolved problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_problem) concerning the sets of [Euclidean distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance)s between points in [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) ==References== [[Category:Measure theory]] [[Category:Dimension theory]] [[Category:Metric geometry]] [[Category:Conjectures]] [[Category:Unsolved problems in geometry]] 08

family of curves is a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) of [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve)s, each of which is given by a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) or [parametrization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parametric_equation) in which one or more of the [parameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameter)s is variable.

fan triangulation is a simple way to [triangulate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon_triangulation) a [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon) by choosing a [vertex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)) and drawing [edges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(geometry)) to all of the other vertices of the polygon.

Fano fibration or Fano fiber space, named after [Gino Fano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gino_Fano), is a morphism of [varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) whose general fiber is a [Fano variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano_variety) (in other words has [ample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ample_line_bundle) [anticanonical bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticanonical_bundle)) of positive dimension.

farthest-first traversal of a [compact metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_metric_space) is a sequence of points in the space, where the first point is selected arbitrarily and each successive point is as far as possible from the set of previously-selected points.
fat object is an object in two or more dimensions, whose lengths in the different dimensions are similar.

Fermat curve is the [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) in the [complex projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_projective_plane) defined in [homogeneous coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_coordinates) (X:Y:Z) by the Fermat equation: : ==Fermat varieties== Fermat-style equations in more variables define as [projective varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_varieties) the Fermat varieties.

Feuerbach hyperbola is a [rectangular hyperbola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangular_hyperbola) passing through important [triangle center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle_center)s such as the [incenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incenter), [orthocenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthocenter), [Gergonne point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gergonne_Point), [Nagel point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagel_point), [mittenpunkt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mittenpunkt) and [Schiffler point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schiffler_point).
fibered manifold is a [surjective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surjective_function) [submersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersion_(mathematics)) is then called a bundle atlas.

field of definition of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) V is essentially the smallest [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) to which the coefficients of the [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s defining V can belong.

field with one element is a suggestive name for an object that should behave similarly to a [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field) with a single element, if such a field could exist.

fieldtree is a [hierarchical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchical) [data structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure) that is used to [index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database_index) [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric) objects.
filling radius of a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) X is a metric invariant of X.
related: Gromov's systolic inequality for essential manifolds

definition: film plane is the surface of an image recording device such as a camera, upon which the [lens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camera_lens) creates the [focused](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focus_(optics)) image.

finiteness properties of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) are a collection of properties that allow the use of various [algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra) and [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) tools, for example [group cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_cohomology), to study the group.

Finsler manifold is a [differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold) where a (possibly [asymmetric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymmetric_norm)) [Minkowski norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski_functional) is provided on each tangent space {{math|T s there always exist shorter curves from γ(0) to γ(t) near γ, as in the [Riemannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) case.

Finsler–Hadwiger theorem is statement in [Euclidean plane geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane_geometry) that describes a third square derived from any two [square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square)s that share a [vertex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)).

first fundamental form is the [inner product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product) on the [tangent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_space) of a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(differential_geometry)) in three-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) which is induced [canonically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_form) from the [dot product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_product) of {{math|R [[Category:Differential geometry of surfaces]] [[Category:Differential geometry]] [[Category:Surfaces]] qkl9oh5s1f7s685bz6cc3hobnaljoy0

first Hurwitz triplet is a triple of distinct [Hurwitz surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_surface)s with the identical [automorphism group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism_group) of the lowest possible genus, namely 14 (genera 3 and 7 each admit a unique Hurwitz surface, respectively the [Klein quartic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klein_quartic) and the [Macbeath surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macbeath_surface)).
first variation of area formula is a fundamental computation for how this quantity is affected by the deformation of the submanifold.

five-dimensional (5D) space is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_(mathematics)) or [physical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_(physics)) space that has five independent [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)s.

definition: fixed point of an isometry group is a point that is a [fixed point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_point_(mathematics)) for every [isometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry) in the group.
fixed-radius near neighbor problem is a variant of the [nearest neighbor search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search) problem.

flag is a sequence of [faces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_(geometry)) of a [polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_polytope), each contained in the next, with exactly one face from each [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension).
flat is an [affine subspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_subspace), i.e.
flat convergence is a notion for convergence of submanifolds of Euclidean space.
flat topology is a [Grothendieck topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_topology) used in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).
flatness is an important geometric condition for [workpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workpiece)s and [tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_tool).

Flattening is a measure of the compression of a [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle) or [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) along a diameter to form an [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse) or an [ellipsoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipsoid) of revolution ([spheroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spheroid)) respectively.

definition: flexagons are [flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) models, usually constructed by folding strips of paper, that can be flexed or folded in certain ways to reveal faces besides the two that were originally on the back and front.

flips and flops are codimension-2 [surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgery_theory) operations arising in the [minimal model program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_model_program), given by [blowing up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blowing_up) along a [relative canonical ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_canonical_model).

flip graph is a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) whose [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(graph_theory)) are [combinatorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics) or [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) objects, and whose [edges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(graph_theory)) link two of these objects when they can be obtained from one another by an elementary operation called a flip.
focuses or foci ( or ; : focus) are special points with reference to which any of a variety of [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve)s is constructed.

formal holomorphic function along a subvariety V of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) W is an algebraic analog of a [holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function) defined in a neighborhood of V.

formal moduli are an aspect of the theory of [moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space)s (of [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_varieties) or [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle)s, for example), closely linked to [deformation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_theory) and [formal geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_geometry).
formal scheme is a type of space which includes data about its surroundings.

Fortune's algorithm is a [sweep line algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweep_line_algorithm) for generating a [Voronoi diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voronoi_diagram) from a set of points in a plane using [O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation)(n Weighted sites may be used to control the areas of the Voronoi cells when using Voronoi diagrams to construct [treemap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treemap)s.
Foundations of geometry is the study of [geometries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometries) as [axiomatic system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiomatic_system)s.

Fourier–Deligne transform, or ℓ-adic Fourier transform, or geometric Fourier transform, is an operation on objects of the [derived category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derived_category) of [ℓ-adic sheaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-adic_sheaf) over the affine line.

Fourier–Motzkin elimination, also known as the FME method, is a mathematical [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) for eliminating variables from a [system of linear inequalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_linear_inequalities).

fractional cascading is a technique to speed up a sequence of [binary search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_search)es for the same value in a sequence of related data structures.

Franz Aurenhammer (born 25 September 1957) is an Austrian [computational geometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry) known for his research in [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry) on [Voronoi diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voronoi_diagram)s, [straight skeleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_skeleton)s, and related structures.
Fredholm module is a mathematical structure used to quantize the [differential calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_calculus).

free factor complex (sometimes also called the complex of free factors) is a [free group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_group) counterpart of the notion of the [curve complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve_complex) of a finite type surface.
free-form deformation (FFD) is a geometric technique used to model simple [deformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_(engineering))s of rigid objects.

Frobenioid is a [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) with some extra structure that generalizes the theory of [line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_bundle)s on models of finite extensions of [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field)s.

Frobenius splitting, introduced by , is a splitting of the [injective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injective_function) [morphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphism) O 0) of [ample line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ample_line_bundle)s L vanishes.

Fréchet distance is a [measure of similarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_of_similarity) between [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve)s that takes into account the location and ordering of the points along the curves.

Fréchet surface is an [equivalence class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_class) of [parametrized surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parametrized_surface)s in a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space).

Fröberg conjecture is a [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) about the possible [Hilbert function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_series_and_Hilbert_polynomial)s of a set of forms.

Frölicher–Nijenhuis bracket is an extension of the [Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields) of [vector fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_fields) to [vector-valued differential form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector-valued_differential_form)s on a [differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold).

Fubini–Study metric (IPA: /fubini-ʃtuːdi/) is a [Kähler metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kähler_metric) on a [complex projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_projective_space) CP ==See also== * [Non-linear sigma model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-linear_sigma_model) * [Kaluza–Klein theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaluza–Klein_theory) * [Arakelov height](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arakelov_height) ==References== * * * * .

definition: Fuchsian model is a representation of a hyperbolic [Riemann surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_surface) R as a quotient of the [upper half-plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_half-plane) H by a [Fuchsian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuchsian_group).
Fujita's conjecture is a problem in the theories of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) and [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold)s.

Fulton–Hansen connectedness theorem is a result from [intersection theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_theory) in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry), for the case of [subvarieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subvariety_(algebraic_geometry)) of [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) with [codimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codimension) large enough to make the intersection have components of dimension at least 1.

functor represented by a scheme X is a set-valued [contravariant functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contravariant_functor) on the [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) of [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics))s such that the value of the functor at each scheme S is (up to natural [bijections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijection), or one-to-one correspondence) the set of all [morphisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphism_of_schemes) == See also == *[Moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space) *[Weil restriction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_restriction) *

fundamental plane in a [spherical coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_coordinate_system) is a [plane of reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_of_reference) that divides the [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) into two [hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere)s.

fundamental theorem of [Riemannian geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_geometry) states that on any [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) (or [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold)) there is a unique [affine connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_connection) that is [torsion-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torsion_(differential_geometry)) and metric-compatible, called the [Levi-Civita connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi-Civita_connection) or Riemannian connection of the given metric.

fundamental vector fields are instruments that describe the infinitesimal behaviour of a smooth [Lie group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group_action) on a [[Differentiable manifold#Definition|smooth manifold]].

Funk transform (also known as Minkowski–Funk transform, Funk–Radon transform or spherical Radon transform) is an [integral transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_transform) defined by integrating a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) on [great circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_circle)s of the [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere).

Futura is a [[Sans-serif#Classification|geometric sans-serif]] [typeface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typeface) designed by [Paul Renner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Renner_(type_designer)) and released in 1927.
fuzzy sphere is one of the simplest and most canonical examples of [non-commutative geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-commutative_geometry).

Følner sequence for a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) is a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence) of [sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) satisfying a particular condition.

Galactic Center is the [barycenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barycenter) of the [Milky Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milky_Way) and a corresponding point on the [rotational axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_axis) of the galaxy.

Galois geometry (named after the 19th-century French [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) [Évariste Galois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Évariste_Galois)) is the branch of [finite geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_geometry) that is concerned with [algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) and [analytic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_geometry) over a [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field) (or Galois field).

gauge covariant derivative is a means of expressing how [fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(physics)) vary from place to place, in a way that respects how the coordinate systems used to describe a physical phenomenon can themselves change from place to place.

gauge group is a group of [gauge symmetries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_symmetry_(mathematics)) of the [Yang–Mills gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang–Mills_theory) of [principal connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_connection)s on a [principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle).

gauge theory is the general study of [connections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_(mathematics)) on [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle)s, [principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)s, and [fibre bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibre_bundle)s.

Gauge theory gravity (GTG) is a theory of [gravitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitation) cast in the mathematical language of [geometric algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_algebra).
Gauss curvature flow is a [geometric flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_flow) for oriented hypersurfaces of [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold)s.

Gauss map of a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(topology)) is a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) that maps each point in the surface to its [normal direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_direction), a [unit vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_vector) that is [orthogonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal) to the surface at that point.

Gauss's lemma asserts that any sufficiently small [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) centered at a point in a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) is perpendicular to every [geodesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic) through the point.

Gaussian correlation inequality (GCI), formerly known as the Gaussian correlation conjecture (GCC), is a [mathematical theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_theorem) in the fields of [mathematical statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_statistics) and [convex geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_geometry).
Gaussian period is a certain kind of sum of [roots of unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_unity).

Gauss–Bonnet theorem (or Gauss–Bonnet formula) is a fundamental formula which links the [curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature) of a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(topology)) to its underlying [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology).

General Dynamics–Boeing AFTI/F-111A Aardvark is a research aircraft modified from a [General Dynamics F-111 Aardvark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Dynamics_F-111_Aardvark) to test a [Boeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing)-built [supercritical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercritical_airfoil) [mission adaptive wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptive_compliant_wing) (MAW).
general elephant is an idiosyncratic name for a general element of the anticanonical system of a variety, introduced by [Miles Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Reid).
general position is a notion of [genericity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generic_property) for a set of points, or other geometric objects.

generalised metric is a generalisation of that of a [metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space), in which the distance is not a [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) but taken from an arbitrary [ordered field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_field).

generalized complex structure is a property of a [differential manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_manifold) that includes as special cases a [complex structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_complex_structure) and a [symplectic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_structure).

generalized flag variety (or simply flag variety) is a [homogeneous space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_space) whose points are [flags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_(linear_algebra)) in a finite-dimensional [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space) V over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) F.

generalized Poincaré conjecture is a statement that a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) that is a [homotopy sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopy_sphere) a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere).
generalized polygon is an [incidence structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_structure) introduced by [Jacques Tits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Tits) in 1959.

generalized quadrangle is an [incidence structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_structure) whose main feature is the lack of any ([non-degenerate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degeneracy_(mathematics))) [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle)s yet containing many [quadrangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_quadrangle)s.
extended Riemann hypothesis (ERH) and when it is formulated for Dirichlet L-functions, it is known as the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH).
Generalizations of trigonometric functions are often developed by starting with one of the above methods and adapting it to a situation other than the real numbers of Euclidean geometry.

generatrix () or describent is a [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)), [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve) or [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)) that, when moved along a given path, generates a new [shape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape).

generic flatness and generic freeness state that under certain hypotheses, a [sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_(mathematics)) of [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics))s on a [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) is [flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_morphism) or [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_module).

generic point P of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) X is a point in a [general position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_position), at which all [generic properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generic_property) are true, a generic property being a property which is true for [almost every](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_everywhere) point.

genus of a multiplicative sequence is a [ring homomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_homomorphism) from the [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) of smooth [compact manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_manifold)s up to the equivalence of bounding a smooth manifold with boundary (i.e., up to suitable [cobordism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobordism)) to another ring, usually the [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number)s, having the property that they are constructed from a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence) of polynomials in [characteristic classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_classes) that arise as coefficients in formal [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series) with good multiplicative properties.

definition: Geoffrey Clarke (28 November 1924 – 30 October 2014) was a British sculptor of ecclesiastical art and maker of stained glass.

Geometriae Dedicata is a [mathematical journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_journal), founded in 1972, concentrating on [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) and its relationship to [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology), [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory) and the theory of [dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system)s.

geometric algebra (also known as a [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra)) is an [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra_over_a_field) that can represent and manipulate geometrical objects such as [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_(mathematics_and_physics))s.

Geometric analysis is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) discipline where tools from [differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_equation)s, especially [elliptic partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_partial_differential_equation)s (PDEs), are used to establish new results in [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry) and [differential topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_topology).

Geometric and Functional Analysis (GAFA) is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) journal published by [Birkhäuser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhäuser), an independent division of [Springer-Verlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springer-Verlag).

geometric class field theory is an extension of [class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_field_theory) to higher-dimensional geometrical objects: much the same way as class field theory describes the [abelianization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelianization) of the [Galois group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_group) of a [local](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field) or [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field), geometric class field theory describes the abelianized [fundamental group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group) of higher dimensional [schemes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) in terms of data related to [algebraic cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_cycle)s.
Geometric combinatorics is a branch of [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) in general and [combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics) in particular.
Geometrical design (GD) is a branch of [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry).

geometric flow, also called a geometric evolution equation, is a type of [partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation) for a geometric object such as a [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric) or an [embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embedded_submanifold).

Geometric graph theory in the broader sense is a large and amorphous subfield of [graph theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_theory), concerned with [graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) defined by [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric) means.

geometric group action is a certain type of [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) of a [discrete group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_group) on a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space).

Geometric group theory is an area in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) devoted to the study of [finitely generated group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group)s via exploring the connections between [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra)ic properties of such [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) and [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) and [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) properties of spaces on which these groups can [act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) non-trivially (that is, when the groups in question are realized as geometric symmetries or continuous transformations of some spaces).

geometric hashing is a method for efficiently finding two-dimensional objects represented by discrete points that have undergone an [affine transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_transformation), though extensions exist to other object representations and transformations.

geometric logic is an [infinitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinitary) generalisation of coherent logic, a restriction of [first-order logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-order_logic) due to [Skolem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skolem) that is [proof-theoretic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof-theoretic)ally tractable.

right triangle altitude theorem or geometric mean theorem is a relation between the [altitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_(triangle)) on the [hypotenuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypotenuse) in a [right triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_triangle) and the two line segments it creates on the hypotenuse.

geometric measure theory (GMT) is the study of [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) properties of [sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) (typically in [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space)) through [measure theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_(mathematics)).

Geometric mechanics is a branch of mathematics applying particular geometric methods to many areas of [mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanics), from mechanics of particles and [rigid bodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_body_mechanics) to [fluid mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_mechanics) and [control theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_theory).

Geometric modeling is a branch of [applied mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_mathematics) and [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry) that studies methods and [algorithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms) for the mathematical description of [shapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape_(mathematics)).

Geometric phase analysis is a method of [digital signal processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_signal_processing) used to determine crystallographic quantities such as d-spacing or strain from [high-resolution transmission electron microscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-resolution_transmission_electron_microscopy) images.

geometric separator is a line (or another shape) that partitions a collection of geometric shapes into two subsets, such that proportion of shapes in each subset is bounded, and the number of shapes that do not belong to any subset (i.e.

geometric series is a [series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Series_(mathematics)) summing the terms of an infinite [geometric sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_sequence), in which the ratio of consecutive terms is constant.
geometric set cover problem is the special case of the [set cover problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_cover_problem) in geometric settings.

geometric spanner or a -spanner graph or a -spanner was initially introduced as a [weighted graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_graph) over a set of points as its vertices for which there is a -path between any pair of vertices for a fixed parameter .

Geometric tomography is a mathematical field that focuses on problems of reconstructing homogeneous (often [convex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polytope)) objects from tomographic data (this might be X-rays, projections, sections, brightness functions, or covariograms).

geometric topology is the study of [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s and [[Map (mathematics)#Maps as functions|maps]] between them, particularly [embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embedding)s of one manifold into another.

geometric transformation is any [bijection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijection) of a [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) to itself (or to another such set) with some salient [geometrical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) underpinning, such as preserving distances, [angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle)s, or ratios (scale).

Geometrical crystallography before X-rays describes how geometrical [crystallography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystallography) developed as a science up to the discovery of [X-rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-rays) by [Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Conrad_Röntgen) in 1895.

geometrically regular ring is a [Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(algebra)) that remains a [regular ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_ring) after any [finite extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_extension) of the base field.

geometrothermodynamics (GTD) is a formalism developed in 2007 by Hernando Quevedo to describe the properties of [thermodynamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermodynamic) systems in terms of concepts of [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry).

Geometry C is a [battery electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_electric_vehicle) [compact crossover SUV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_crossover_SUV) produced by Chinese manufacturer [Geely Auto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geely_Auto) under the [Geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry_(car_marque)) brand.

The Geometry Center was a [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) research and education center at the [University of Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota).
Geometry Expert (GEX) is a Chinese software package for dynamic diagram drawing and automated geometry theorem proving and discovering.

Geometry of numbers, also known as geometric number theory, is the part of [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory) which uses [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) for the study of [algebraic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number)s.

George Peacock [FRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow_of_the_Royal_Society) (9 April 1791 – 8 November 1858) was an English [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) and [Anglican cleric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_cleric).

definition: Geospatial topology is the study and application of qualitative [spatial relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spatial_relation)ships between [geographic feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_feature)s, or between representations of such features in [geographic information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_data_and_information), such as in [geographic information system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_information_system)s (GIS).

Gerstenhaber algebra (sometimes called an antibracket algebra or braid algebra) is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) discovered by [Murray Gerstenhaber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murray_Gerstenhaber) (1963) that combines the structures of a [supercommutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercommutative_ring) and a [graded Lie superalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graded_Lie_superalgebra).

GEUP is a commercial [interactive geometry software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interactive_geometry_software) program on windows, similar to [Cabri Geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabri_Geometry).
Gieseking manifold is a cusped [hyperbolic 3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_3-manifold) of finite volume.

Gilbert–Pollak conjecture is an unproven [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) on the ratio of lengths of [Steiner tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_tree)s and [Euclidean minimum spanning tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_minimum_spanning_tree)s for the same point sets in the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane).

girth of a geometric object, in a certain direction, is the [perimeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perimeter) of its [parallel projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_projection) in that direction.

GJMS operators are a family of [differential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_operator)s, that are defined on a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold).

GKM variety is a [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) equipped with a [torus action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torus_action) that meets certain conditions.

definition: edge graph (also known as vertex-edge graph or just graph) of a [polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope) is a combinatorial [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(graph_theory)) whose vertices and edges correspond directly to the [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)) and [edges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(geometry)) of the polytope.

graph of groups is an object consisting of a collection of [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) indexed by the vertices and edges of a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)), together with a family of [monomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monomorphism)s of the edge groups into the vertex groups.

Graphical Models is an [academic journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal) in [computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_graphics) and [geometry processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry_processing) publisher by [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier).

Graphs and Combinatorics (ISSN 0911-0119, abbreviated Graphs Combin.) is a [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_review) [academic journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal) in [graph theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_theory), [combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics), and [discrete geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_geometry) published by [Springer Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springer_Science+Business_Media).

Grassmann d-plane bundle of a vector bundle E on an [algebraic scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_scheme) X is a scheme over X: : , which is the relative version of the [Euler sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_sequence).

Grauert's approximation theorem, due to [Grauert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Grauert), is an analog of Whitney’s approximation theorem for [real-analytic map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-analytic_map)s.

Grauert–Riemenschneider vanishing theorem is an extension of the [Kodaira vanishing theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira_vanishing_theorem) on the vanishing of higher [cohomology group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_group)s of [coherent sheaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf) on a compact [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold), due to .

great circle or orthodrome is the [circular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle) [intersection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_(geometry)) of a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) and a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) [passing through](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_(geometry)) the sphere's [center point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_(geometry)).

great ellipse is an [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse) passing through two [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) on a [spheroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spheroid) and having the same [center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_(geometry)) as that of the spheroid.

great-circle distance, orthodromic distance, or spherical distance is the [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance) between two [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) on a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere), measured along the [great-circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_circle) arc between them.

greedy embedding is a process of assigning coordinates to the nodes of a [telecommunications network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications_network) in order to allow [greedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greedy_algorithm) [geographic routing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_routing) to be used to route messages within the network.

greedy geometric spanner is an [undirected graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undirected_graph) whose distances approximate the [Euclidean distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance)s among a [finite set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_set) of points in a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space).

Gridnik is a [geometrical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometrical) [sans serif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sans_serif) [typeface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typeface) designed by Dutch [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design)er [Wim Crouwel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wim_Crouwel) in 1974.

Grigorchuk group or the first Grigorchuk group is a [finitely generated group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group) constructed by [Rostislav Grigorchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rostislav_Grigorchuk) that provided the first example of a [finitely generated group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group) of intermediate (that is, faster than polynomial but slower than exponential) [growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growth_rate_(group_theory)).

Gromov boundary of a [δ-hyperbolic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Δ-hyperbolic_space) (especially a [hyperbolic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_group)) is an abstract concept generalizing the boundary sphere of [hyperbolic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_space).

Gromov product is a concept in the theory of [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space)s named after the mathematician [Mikhail Gromov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gromov_(mathematician)).

definition: Gromov–Hausdorff convergence, named after [Mikhail Gromov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gromov_(mathematician)) and [Felix Hausdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Hausdorff), is a notion for convergence of [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space)s which is a generalization of [Hausdorff distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_distance).

Gromov–Witten (GW) invariants are [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number)s that, in certain situations, count the number of curves ([pseudoholomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoholomorphic_curve) or [algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve)) meeting prescribed conditions in a given ambient space (a [symplectic manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_manifold) or a smooth [projective variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_variety)).
Grothendieck connection is a way of viewing [connections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_(mathematics)) in terms of descent data from infinitesimal neighbourhoods of the diagonal.
Grothendieck's connectedness theorem, It is a local analogue of [Bertini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertini's_theorem).

Grothendieck's Galois theory is an abstract approach to the [Galois theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_theory) of fields, developed around 1960 to provide a way to study the [fundamental group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_group) of [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology) in the setting of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).

Grothendieck–Katz p-curvature conjecture is a [local-global principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local-global_principle) for [linear ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_differential_equation)s, related to [differential Galois theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_Galois_theory) and in a loose sense analogous to the result in the [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem) considered as the [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) case.
ground field is a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K fixed at the beginning of the discussion.

Group analysis of differential equations is a branch of mathematics that studies the symmetry properties of [differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_equation)s with respect to various transformations of independent and dependent variables.
group functor is a group-valued functor on the category of commutative rings.
action of a group scheme is a generalization of a [group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) to a [group scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_scheme).

groupoid object is both a generalization of a [groupoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupoid) which is built on richer structures than sets, and a generalization of a [group object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_object)s when the multiplication is only [partially defined](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_function).

Groups, Geometry, and Dynamics is a quarterly [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed) [mathematics journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_journal) published quarterly by the [European Mathematical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Mathematical_Society).

growth rate of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) with respect to a symmetric [generating set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_set_of_a_group) describes how fast a group grows.

Grushko theorem or the Grushko–Neumann theorem is a theorem stating that the [rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rank_of_a_group) (that is, the smallest [cardinality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinality) of a [generating set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_set_of_a_group)) of a [free product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_product) of two groups is equal to the sum of the ranks of the two free factors.

Gröbner fan of an [ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_(ring_theory)) in the [ring of polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_ring) is a concept in the theory of [Gröbner bases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gröbner_basis).

Grünbaum–Rigby configuration is a symmetric [configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Configuration_(geometry)) consisting of 21 points and 21 lines, with four points on each line and four lines through each point.

Gudkov's conjecture, also called Gudkov’s congruence, (named after [Dmitry Gudkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitry_Gudkov_(mathematician))) was a [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture), and is now a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem), which states that a [M-curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harnack's_curve_theorem) of [even](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_(mathematics)) degree ==See also== *[Hilbert's sixteenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert's_sixteenth_problem) *[Tropical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_geometry) ==References== [[Category:Conjectures that have been prove
Guillotine cutting is the process of producing small rectangular items of fixed dimensions from a given large rectangular sheet, using only guillotine-cuts.

Guillotine partition is the process of partitioning a [rectilinear polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectilinear_polygon), possibly containing some holes, into rectangles, using only guillotine-cuts.

gyration is a [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation) in a [discrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_group) [subgroup of symmetries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_group) of the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane) such that the subgroup does not also contain a [reflection symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflection_symmetry) whose axis passes through the center of [rotational symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_symmetry).
gyrovector space is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) concept proposed by Abraham A.

gömböc () is any member of a class of [convex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set), [three-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional) and [homogeneous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous) bodies that are mono-monostatic, meaning that they have just one stable and one unstable [point of equilibrium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_equilibrium) when resting on a flat surface.

h topology is a [Grothendieck topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_topology) introduced by [Vladimir Voevodsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Voevodsky) to study the [homology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_theory) of [schemes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)).

Haagerup property, named after [Uffe Haagerup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uffe_Haagerup) and also known as [Gromov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gromov_(mathematician))'s a-T-menability, is a property of [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics))s that is a strong negation of [Kazhdan's property (T)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhdan's_property_(T)).
Hadamard space, named after [Jacques Hadamard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Hadamard), is a non-linear generalization of a [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space).

Haefliger structure on a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) is a generalization of a [foliation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foliation) of a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold), introduced by [André Haefliger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/André_Haefliger) in 1970.

Haken manifold is a [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space), [P²-irreducible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P2-irreducible_manifold) [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold) that is sufficiently large, meaning that it contains a properly embedded [two-sided](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2-sided) [incompressible surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incompressible_surface).

half-side formula relates the angles and lengths of the sides of [spherical triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_triangle)s, which are triangles drawn on the [surface of a sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_geometry) and so have curved sides and do not obey the formulas for [plane triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle)s.

half-space is either of the two parts into which a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) divides the three-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space).

Hall plane is a [non-Desarguesian projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Desarguesian_projective_plane) constructed by [Marshall Hall Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Hall_(mathematician)) (1943).
Hamiltonian field theory is the field-theoretic analogue to classical [Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics).

Hamiltonian vector field on a [symplectic manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_manifold) is a [vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_field) defined for any energy function or Hamiltonian.

Hamilton–Jacobi equation, named after [William Rowan Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rowan_Hamilton) and [Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Gustav_Jacob_Jacobi), is an alternative formulation of [classical mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_mechanics), equivalent to other formulations such as [Newton's laws of motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton's_laws_of_motion), [Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics) and [Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics).

Hanan grid of a [finite set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_set) of points in [the plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) is obtained by constructing vertical and horizontal lines through each point in .

Hanan Samet is a [Computer Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Science) researcher and Distinguished University Professor at the [University of Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland)'s Computer Science Department, which is part of the [University of Maryland College of Computer, Mathematical, and Natural Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland_College_of_Computer,_Mathematical,_and_Natural_Sciences).

hand compass (also hand bearing compass or sighting compass) is a compact magnetic [compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass) capable of one-hand use and fitted with a sighting device to record a precise [bearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bearing_(navigation)) or [azimuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azimuth) to a given target or to determine a location.
Handel Gothic is a [[Sans-serif#Geometric|geometric]] [sans-serif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sans-serif) typeface designed in 1965 by Donald J.
handle decomposition of an m-[manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) M is a union .

Hansen's problem is a problem in planar [surveying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveying), named after the astronomer [Peter Andreas Hansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Andreas_Hansen) (1795 If one of these fractions has a denominator close to zero, use the other one.

Harborth's conjecture states that every [planar graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planar_graph) has a planar [drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_drawing) in which every edge is a straight [segment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_segment) of [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) length.

harmonic coordinates are a certain kind of [coordinate chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_chart) on a [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold), determined by a [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric) on the manifold.
harmonic morphism is a (smooth) map is a harmonic morphism.

Hartshorne ellipse is an [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse) in the [unit ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_ball) bounded by the [4-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4-sphere) S .

Hasse–Weil zeta function attached to an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) V defined over an [algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number_field) K is a [meromorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meromorphic_function) on the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane) defined in terms of the number of points on the variety after reducing modulo each prime number p.
Hatch marks (also called hash marks or tick marks) are a form of [mathematical notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_notation).

Hauptvermutung of [geometric topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_topology) is a now refuted conjecture asking whether any two [triangulations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulation_(topology)) of a [triangulable space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulable_space) have subdivisions that are combinatorially equivalent, i.e.

Hausdorff measure is a generalization of the traditional notions of [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area) and [volume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume) to non-integer dimensions, specifically [fractals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractals) and their [Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension)s.

heat kernel signature (HKS) is a feature descriptor for use in deformable [shape analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape_analysis_(digital_geometry)) and belongs to the group of [spectral shape analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_shape_analysis) methods.

hedgehog or plane hedgehog is a type of [plane curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_curve), the [envelope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(mathematics)) of a family of lines determined by a [support function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Support_function).

Heegaard splitting () is a decomposition of a compact oriented [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold) that results from dividing it into two [handlebodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handlebody).
Heesch number of a shape is the maximum number of layers of copies of the same shape that can surround it with no overlaps and no gaps.
height function is a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) that quantifies the complexity of mathematical objects.

Heine–Cantor theorem states that a [continuous function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function) between two [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space)s is uniformly continuous if its domain is [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space).
helix (; ) is a shape like a cylindrical [coil spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coil_spring) or the thread of a [machine screw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_screw).

Helly family of order is a family of [sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) in which every minimal subfamily with an empty [intersection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_(set_theory)) has or fewer sets in it.

Helly's theorem is a basic result in [discrete geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_geometry) on the [intersection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_(set_theory)) of [convex set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set)s.

hemihelix is a curved geometric shape consisting of a series of [helices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helix) with alternating [chirality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirality), connected by a [perversion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tendril_perversion) at the reversals.
Henneberg surface is a [non-orientable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-orientable) [minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface) V.
