definition: heptadecagon, septadecagon or 17-gon is a seventeen-sided [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon).
Hermite's cotangent identity is a [trigonometric identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_identity) discovered by [Charles Hermite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Hermite).
Hermitian manifold is the complex analogue of a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold).
Hermitian symmetric space is a [Hermitian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_manifold) which at every point has an inversion symmetry preserving the Hermitian structure.

Hermitian Yang–Mills connection (or Hermite–Einstein connection) is a Chern connection associated to an inner product on a [holomorphic vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_vector_bundle) over a [Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kähler_manifold) that satisfies an analogue of Einstein's equations: namely, the contraction of the curvature 2-form of the connection with the Kähler form is required to be a constant times the identity transformation.

Heronian triangle (or Heron triangle) is a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) whose side lengths , , and and [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area) are all positive [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer)s.
Herschel's condition is a condition for an [optical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_system) to produce sharp images for objects over an extended axial range, i.e.

Hesse's theorem, named for [Otto Hesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Hesse), states that if two pairs of opposite vertices of a [quadrilateral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrilateral) are conjugate with respect to some conic, then so is the third pair.

Hessian pair or Hessian duad, named for [Otto Hesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Hesse), is a pair of points of the [projective line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_line) canonically associated with a set of 3 points of the projective line.

hexafoil is a design with six-fold [dihedral symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dihedral_group) composed from six [vesica piscis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesica_piscis) lenses arranged radially around a central point, often shown enclosed in a circumference of another six lenses.

Hierarchical Triangular Mesh (HTM) is a kind of [quad tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadtree) based on subdivision of a distorted [octahedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahedron), used for [mesh generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesh_generation) in [3-D computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics) and [geometric data structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_data_analysis).

higher gauge theory is the general study of counterparts of [gauge theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory) that involve higher-degree differential forms instead of the traditional [connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_(mathematics)) 1-forms of [Yang-Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang-Mills) gauge theories.
higher stack is a [higher category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_category) generalization of a [stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(mathematics)) (a category-valued sheaf).

Hilbert basis of a [convex cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_cone) C is a minimal set of integer [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_(mathematics))s in C such that every [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) vector in C is a [conical combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conical_combination) of the vectors in the Hilbert basis with integer coefficients.
Hilbert manifold is a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) modeled on [Hilbert spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_spaces).

Hilbert metric, also known as the Hilbert projective metric, is an explicitly defined [distance function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_(mathematics)) on a bounded [convex subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set) of the n-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) R , endowed with its Hilbert metric, to be a [Gromov hyperbolic space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gromov_hyperbolic_space).

Hilbert scheme is a [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_theory) that is the parameter space for the [closed subscheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_subscheme)s of some projective space (or a more general projective scheme), refining the [Chow variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_variety).

Hilbert function, the Hilbert polynomial, and the Hilbert series of a [graded commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graded_algebra) finitely generated over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) are three strongly related notions which measure the growth of the dimension of the homogeneous components of the algebra.

Hilbert's eighteenth problem is [one of the 23 problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_problems) set out in a celebrated list compiled in 1900 by mathematician [David Hilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hilbert).

Hilbert's fifteenth problem is one of the 23 [Hilbert problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_problems) set out in a list compiled in 1900 by [David Hilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hilbert).

definition: Hilbert–Smith conjecture is concerned with the [transformation group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_group)s of [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s; and in particular with the limitations on [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group)s G that can act effectively (faithfully) on a (topological) manifold M.

Kuga fiber variety, introduced by , is a [fiber space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_bundle) whose fibers are [abelian varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety) and whose base space is an [arithmetic quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_variety) of a [Hermitian symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_symmetric_space).

Kulkarni–Nomizu product (named for [Ravindra Shripad Kulkarni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravindra_Shripad_Kulkarni) and [Katsumi Nomizu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsumi_Nomizu)) is defined for two -[tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor)s and gives as a result a -tensor.

Kummer configuration, named for [Ernst Kummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Kummer), is a [geometric configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_configuration) of 16 points and 16 planes such that each point lies on 6 of the planes and each plane contains 6 of the points.
Kunstweg is a set of [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm)s developed by [Jost Bürgi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jost_Bürgi) in the late 16th century.

Kuratowski convergence or Painlevé-Kuratowski convergence is a notion of [convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_of_a_sequence) for [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset)s of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space).

Kurosh subgroup theorem describes the algebraic structure of [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup)s of [free product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_product)s of [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)).

Kähler identities are a collection of identities between operators on a [Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kähler_manifold) relating the [Dolbeault operators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolbeault_operator) and their [adjoints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_operator), contraction and wedge operators of the [Kähler form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kähler_form), and the [Laplacians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplacian) of the Kähler metric.

Kähler manifold is a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) with three mutually compatible structures: a [complex structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold), a [Riemannian structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold), and a [symplectic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_manifold).

Kähler–Einstein metric on a [complex manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold) is a [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric) that is both a [Kähler metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kähler_metric) and an [Einstein metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_manifold).

Lagrangian foliation or polarization is a [foliation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foliation) of a [symplectic manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_manifold), whose leaves are [Lagrangian submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_submanifold)s.

Lagrangian Grassmannian is the [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold) of [Lagrangian subspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_subspace)s of a real [symplectic vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_vector_space) V.

Laguerre plane is one of the three types of [Benz plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benz_plane), which are the [Möbius plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Möbius_plane), Laguerre plane and [Minkowski plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski_plane).
Laguerre–Forsyth invariant is a cubic differential that is an invariant of a projective [plane curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_curve).
Lam's problem is the problem of determining if a [[Projective_plane#Finite_projective_planes|finite projective plane]] of order ten exists.

Lanczos tensor or Lanczos potential is a [rank 3 tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_rank) in [general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity) that generates the [Weyl tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_tensor).

Langevin dynamics is an approach to the mathematical modeling of the [dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(physics)) of molecular systems using the [Langevin equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langevin_equation).

Laplace functional refers to one of two possible mathematical functions of functions or, more precisely, [functional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_analysis)s that serve as mathematical tools for studying either [point process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_process)es or [concentration of measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_of_measure) properties of [metric spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_spaces).

Laplace–Beltrami operator is a generalization of the [Laplace operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_operator) to functions defined on [submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold)s in [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) and, even more generally, on [Riemannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) and [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold)s.

Large deformation diffeomorphic metric mapping (LDDMM) is a specific suite of algorithms used for diffeomorphic mapping and manipulating dense imagery based on diffeomorphic metric mapping within the academic discipline of [computational anatomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_anatomy), to be distinguished from its precursor based on diffeomorphic mapping.

largest empty sphere problem is the problem of finding a [hypersphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersphere) of largest radius in d-dimensional space whose interior does not overlap with any given obstacles.

lateral surface of a [three-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space) object is the surface of all its sides, excluding its [base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_(geometry)) and top (when they exist).
lattice plane of a given [Bravais lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bravais_lattice) is any plane containing at least three noncollinear Bravais lattice points.

law of sines (sometimes called the sine formula or sine rule) is a mathematical [equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation) relating the [lengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lengths) of the sides of any [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) to the [sine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine)s of its [angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle)s.

ligand close packing theory (LCP theory), sometimes called the ligand close packing model describes how [ligand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligand) – [ligand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligand) repulsions affect the geometry around a central atom.

Le Potier's vanishing theorem is an extension of the [Kodaira vanishing theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodaira_vanishing_theorem), on [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle)s.

Lebesgue's universal covering problem is an unsolved problem in [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) that asks for the [convex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set) shape of smallest area that can cover every planar set of diameter one.

LeBrun manifold is a [connected sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connected_sum) of copies of the [complex projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_projective_plane), equipped with an explicit self-dual metric.
Lee Hwa Chung theorem is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) in [symplectic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_topology).
Lefschetz manifold is a particular kind of [symplectic manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_manifold) ==Notes== [[Category:Symplectic geometry]] 1fg7se2w6wqctddjnkqqqhdhf1u61bp

Lefschetz pencil is a construction in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) considered by [Solomon Lefschetz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_Lefschetz), used to analyse the [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology) of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) It has been shown that Lefschetz pencils exist in [characteristic zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_zero).

Lefschetz theorem on (1,1)-classes, named after [Solomon Lefschetz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_Lefschetz), is a classical statement relating holomorphic [line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_bundle)s on a [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) [Kähler manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kähler_manifold) to classes in its integral [cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology).
Left–right confusion (LRC) is the inability to accurately differentiate between [left and right directions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_and_right_directions).

lemon is a [geometric shape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_shape) that is constructed as the [surface of revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_of_revolution) of a [circular arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_arc) of [angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle) less than half of a full circle rotated about an axis passing through the endpoints of the lens (or arc).
length function is a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) that assigns a number to each element of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)).
lens is a [convex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set) region bounded by two [circular arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_arc)s joined to each other at their endpoints.
Leslie Tillotson Thornton (26 May 1925 – 9 February 2016) was an English sculptor.

level structure on a [space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_(mathematics)) X is an extra structure attached to X that shrinks or eliminates the [automorphism group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism_group) of X, by demanding automorphisms to preserve the level structure; attaching a level structure is often phrased as rigidifying the geometry of X.
Levi graph or incidence graph is a [bipartite graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipartite_graph) associated with an [incidence structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_structure).

Levi-Civita connection is the unique [affine connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_connection) on the [tangent bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_bundle) of a [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) that [preserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_connection) the ([pseudo-](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold))[Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric) and is [torsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torsion_(differential_geometry))-free.

Liberman's lemma is a theorem used in studying [intrinsic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrinsic_metric) of [convex surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_surface).
Lichnerowicz conjecture is a generalization of a conjecture introduced by .
lidinoid is a [triply periodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triply_periodic_minimal_surface) [minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface).

Lie bialgebroid consists of two compatible [Lie algebroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebroid)s defined on dual vector bundles.

Lie–Palais theorem is a partial converse to the fact that any [smooth action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group_action) of a [Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_group) induces an infinitesimal action of its [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra).

Lindisfarne Association (1972–2012) was a nonprofit foundation and diverse group of intellectuals organized by [cultural historian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_history) [William Irwin Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Irwin_Thompson) for the ] [Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times), 20 August 1989.
straight line, usually abbreviated line, is an infinitely long object with no width, depth, or [curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature).

definition: line at infinity is a [projective line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_line) that is added to the [affine plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_plane) in order to give [closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closure_(topology)) to, and remove the exceptional cases from, the [incidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_(geometry)) properties of the resulting [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane).

line coordinates are used to specify the position of a [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)) just as point coordinates (or simply [coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_system)) are used to specify the position of a [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)).
Line fitting is the process of constructing a [straight line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_line) that has the best fit to a series of data points.
Line moiré is one type of [moiré pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moiré_pattern); a pattern that appears when superposing two transparent layers containing correlated opaque patterns.
line of action (also called line of application) of a [force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force) () is a geometric representation of how the force is applied.

definition: line of sight, also known as visual axis or sightline (also sight line), is an [imaginary line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_line) between a viewer/[observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observation)/[[wikt:spectator|spectator]]'s [eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye)(s) and a subject of interest, or their [relative direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_direction_(geometry)).

line segment is a part of a [straight line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(mathematics)) that is bounded by two distinct endpoints (its [extreme point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_point)s), and contains every [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) on the line that is between its endpoints.

Linear programming (LP), also called linear optimization, is a method to achieve the best outcome (such as maximum profit or lowest cost) in a [mathematical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_model) whose requirements and objective are represented by [[linear function#As a polynomial function|linear relationships]].
linear separability is a property of two sets of [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)).
linear space is a basic structure in [incidence geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_geometry).
link in a simplicial complex is a generalization of the [neighborhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighbourhood_(graph_theory)) of a vertex in a graph.

link distance between two points in a [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon) is the minimum number of line segments of any [polygonal chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygonal_chain) within the polygon that has the two points as its endpoints.

Liouville field theory (or simply Liouville theory) is a [two-dimensional conformal field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_conformal_field_theory) whose classical [equation of motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation_of_motion) is a generalization of [Liouville's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville's_equation).

Lissajous curve , also known as Lissajous figure or Bowditch curve , is the graph of a system of [parametric equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parametric_equation)s : Therefore, Lissajous curves have applications in music education by graphically representing differences between intervals and among tuning systems.

Lissajous orbit (), named after [Jules Antoine Lissajous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jules_Antoine_Lissajous), is a [quasi-periodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiperiodicity) orbital trajectory that an object can follow around a [Lagrangian point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_point) of a three-body system with minimal propulsion.

local cohomology is an algebraic analogue of [relative cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_homology).
Local coordinates are the ones used in a local [coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_system) or a local [coordinate space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_space).

Local feature size refers to several related concepts in [computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_graphics) and [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry) for measuring the size of a geometric object near a particular point.
local flatness is a smoothness condition that can be imposed on topological [submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold)s.

logarithmic pair consists of a [variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety), together with a divisor along which one allows mild logarithmic singularities.

low-dimensional topology is the branch of [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) that studies [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s, or more generally topological spaces, of four or fewer [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)s.

Luna's slice theorem, introduced by , describes the local behavior of an action of a [reductive algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductive_algebraic_group) on an [affine variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_variety).

motive (or sometimes motif, following [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language) usage) is an abstract object introduced by [Alexander Grothendieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grothendieck) in the 1960s as part of a proposed universal [cohomology theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohomology_theory) for [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety).
Motivic cohomology is an invariant of [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) and of more general [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics))s.

Motivic integration is a notion in [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) that was introduced by [Maxim Kontsevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxim_Kontsevich) in 1995 and was developed by [Jan Denef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Denef) and [François Loeser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/François_Loeser).

motivic L-functions are a generalization of [Hasse–Weil L-functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse–Weil_L-function) to general [motives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motive_(algebraic_geometry)) over [global field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field)s.
motivic sheaf is a [motivic-cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivic_cohomology) counterpart of an [l-adic sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-adic_sheaf).

motivic zeta function of a [smooth algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_algebraic_variety) This is essentially the [partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_(number_theory)).

Moufang plane, named for [Ruth Moufang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Moufang), is a type of [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane), more specifically a special type of [translation plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_plane).

Moulton plane is an example of an [affine plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_plane_(incidence_geometry)) in which [Desargues's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desargues's_theorem) does not hold.

mountain climbing problem is a [mathematical problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_problem) that considers a two-dimensional mountain range (represented as a [continuous function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function)), and asks whether it is possible for two [mountain climbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering) starting at [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level) on the left and right sides of the mountain to meet at the summit, while maintaining equal altitudes at all times.

moving frame is a flexible generalization of the notion of a [coordinate frame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_frame) (an [ordered basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_basis) of a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space), in conjunction with an [origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_(mathematics))) often used to study the [extrinsic differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry) of [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold)s embedded in a [homogeneous space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_space).

moving sofa problem or sofa problem is a two-dimensional idealization of real-life [furniture-moving problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_planning) and asks for the rigid two-dimensional shape of the largest [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area) that can be maneuvered through an L-shaped planar region with legs of unit width.
Moyal bracket is the suitably normalized antisymmetrization of the phase-space [star product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moyal_product).

Muller–Schupp theorem states that a [finitely generated group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finitely_generated_group) G has [context-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Context-free_language) [word problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_problem_for_groups) if and only if G is virtually free.

multi-homogeneous Bézout theorem is a generalization to multi-homogeneous polynomials of [Bézout's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bézout's_theorem), which counts the number of isolated common zeros of a set of [homogeneous polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_polynomial)s.

multicover bifiltration is a two-parameter sequence of nested [topological spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) derived from the covering of a [finite set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_set) in a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space) by growing [metric balls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_(mathematics)).

multiplicative sequence or m-sequence is a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence) of [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s associated with a formal [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) structure.

Mumford vanishing theorem proved by [Mumford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Mumford) The Mumford vanishing theorem is related to the [Ramanujam vanishing theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujam_vanishing_theorem), and is generalized by the [Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawamata–Viehweg_vanishing_theorem).

Murakami–Yano formula, introduced by , is a formula for the volume of a [hyperbolic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_geometry) or spherical [tetrahedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedron) given in terms of its [dihedral angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dihedral_angles).

Myers's theorem, also known as the Bonnet–Myers theorem, is a celebrated, fundamental theorem in the mathematical field of [Riemannian geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_geometry).

Möbius plane (named after [August Ferdinand Möbius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Ferdinand_Möbius)) is the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane) supplemented by a single [point at infinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_at_infinity).
Möbius transformation of the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane) is a [rational function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_function) of the form Co.

Möbius–Kantor configuration is a [configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Configuration_(geometry)) consisting of eight points and eight lines, with three points on each line and three lines through each point.

Möller–Trumbore ray-triangle intersection algorithm, named after its inventors Tomas Möller and Ben Trumbore, is a fast method for calculating the [intersection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_(Euclidean_geometry)) of a [ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_(geometry)) and a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) in [three dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space) without needing precomputation of the plane equation of the [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) containing the triangle.

n! conjecture is the [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) that the [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension) of a certain [bi-graded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi-graded) [module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Module_(mathematics)) of [diagonal harmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonal_harmonic)s is n!.

-sphere or hypersphere is an -[dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension) generalization of the -dimensional [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle) and -dimensional [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) to any non-negative [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) .
Nadel vanishing theorem is a global [vanishing theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanishing_theorem) for [multiplier ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplier_ideal)s, introduced by A.
N-1 ring is an [integral domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_domain) Sons, New York-London 1962, reprinted by R.

Nakai conjecture is an unproven characterization of [smooth algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_algebraic_variety), [conjectured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjectured) by Japanese mathematician Yoshikazu Nakai in 1961.

napkin folding problem is a problem in [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) and the [mathematics of paper folding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_of_paper_folding) that explores whether folding a [square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_(geometry)) or a [rectangular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangle) [napkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napkin) can increase its [perimeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perimeter).
Napoleon's problem is a [compass construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_and_straightedge) problem.

Nauruan navigational system is a way of expressing direction, similar to [North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North), [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South), [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East) and [West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West), but limitations in the system mean that it is unable to be used outside of [Nauru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nauru).

near-field is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) similar to a [division ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_ring), except that it has only one of the two distributive laws.

nearest neighbor graph (NNG) is a [directed graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_graph) defined for a set of points in a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space), such as the [Euclidean distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance) in [the plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)).

Nearest neighbor search (NNS), as a form of proximity search, is the [optimization problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimization_problem) of finding the point in a given set that is closest (or most similar) to a given point.
nearly Kähler manifold is an [almost Hermitian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_Hermitian_manifold) .
negative pedal curve is a [plane curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_curve) that can be constructed from another plane curve C and a fixed point P.

Neo Sans and Neo Tech are the typefaces designed by the British type designer [Sebastian * [[Rede Telecine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seb_Lester) used Neo Sans on its branding from 2010 until 2019.

Neovius surface is a [triply periodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triply_periodic_minimal_surface) [minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface) originally discovered by Finnish mathematician Edvard Rudolf Neovius (the uncle of [Rolf Nevanlinna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolf_Nevanlinna)).
Nesting algorithms are used to make the [most efficient use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesting_(process)) of material or space.

Neuberg cubic is a special [cubic plane curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_plane_curve) associated with a reference [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) with several remarkable properties.

neusis (; ; plural: ) is a [geometric construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_construction) method that was used in antiquity by [Greek mathematicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mathematics).

Neutraface is a geometric [sans-serif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sans-serif) [typeface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typeface) designed by [Christian Schwartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Schwartz) for [House Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Industries), an American digital [type foundry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_foundry).

neutral plane or neutral surface is a conceptual [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) within a [beam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beam_(structure)) or [cantilever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantilever).

Nevanlinna invariant of an [ample divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ample_divisor) D on a [normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_variety) [projective variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_variety) X is a real number connected with the rate of growth of the number of rational points on the variety with respect to the embedding defined by the divisor.

Newton polytope is an [integral polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_polytope) associated with a multivariate [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) that can be used in the [asymptotic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_analysis) of those polynomials.

Newton's theorem about ovals states that the area cut off by a [secant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secant_line) of a smooth [convex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set) oval is not an [algebraic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_function) of the secant.

Newton–Gauss line (or Gauss–Newton line) is the [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)) joining the [midpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midpoint)s of the three [diagonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonal)s of a [complete quadrilateral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_quadrilateral).

Newton–Okounkov body, also called an Okounkov body, is a [convex body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_body) in [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) associated to a [divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor_(algebraic_geometry)) (or more generally a linear system) on a [variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety).
Nielsen realization problem is a question asked by about whether finite subgroups of mapping class groups can act on surfaces, that was answered positively by .

nilcurve is a pointed [stable curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_curve) over a [finite field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field) with an [indigenous bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_bundle) whose [p-curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-curvature) is square nilpotent.

nilmanifold is a [differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold) which has a [transitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitive_(group_action)) [nilpotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilpotent_group) group of [diffeomorphisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffeomorphisms) acting on it.

nine-point conic of a [complete quadrangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_quadrangle) is a [conic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conic_section) that passes through the three diagonal points and the six [midpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midpoint)s of sides of the complete quadrangle.

Nisnevich topology, sometimes called the completely decomposed topology, is a [Grothendieck topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_topology) on the category of [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics))s which has been used in [algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory), [A¹ homotopy theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A¹_homotopy_theory), and the theory of [motive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motive_(algebraic_geometry))s.
Noether normalization lemma is a result of [commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra), introduced by [Emmy Noether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Noether) in 1926.

non-Archimedean ordered field is an [ordered field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_field) that does not satisfy the [Archimedean property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedean_property).

non-Desarguesian plane is a [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane) (or sometimes an [affine plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_plane)) that does not satisfy [Desargues' theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desargues'_theorem) (named after [Girard Desargues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girard_Desargues)), or in other words a plane that is not a [Desarguesian plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desarguesian_plane).

non-Euclidean geometry consists of two geometries based on [axiom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom)s closely related to those that specify [Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry).
non-squeezing theorem, also called Gromov's non-squeezing theorem, is one of the most important theorems in [symplectic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_geometry).

nonlinear partial differential equation is a [partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation) with [nonlinear terms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_system).

nonmetricity tensor in [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry) is the [covariant derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_derivative) of the [metric tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_tensor).

definition: one-dimensional symmetry group is a [mathematical group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) that describes [symmetries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry) in one dimension (1D).
one-relator group is a group given by a [group presentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_presentation) with a single defining relation.
Ooguri–Vafa metric is a four-dimensional [Hyperkähler metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperkähler_metric).

open book decomposition (or simply an open book) is a [decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold_decomposition) of a [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_manifold) [oriented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriented) [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold) M into a union of [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(topology))s (necessarily with boundary) and [solid tori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_torus).

open-chain compound (or open chain compound) or acyclic compound (Greek prefix α 'without' and κύκλος 'cycle') is a compound with a linear structure, rather than a [cyclic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_compound) one.

orbital hybridisation (or hybridization) is the concept of mixing [atomic orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_orbital)s to form new hybrid orbitals (with different energies, shapes, etc., than the component atomic orbitals) suitable for the pairing of electrons to form [chemical bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_bond)s in [valence bond theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_bond_theory).

orbital node is either of the two points where an [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit)ing object [intersects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_(Euclidean_geometry)) a [plane of reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_of_reference) inclined with respect to the [orbital plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_plane).
orbital overlap is the concentration of [orbitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_orbital) on adjacent atoms in the same regions of space.
orbital plane of a revolving body is the [geometric plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) in which its [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit) lies.

orbital plane of reference (or orbital reference plane) is the [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_planes_in_three-dimensional_space) used to define [orbital elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_elements) (positions).

order-4 120-cell honeycomb is one of five compact [regular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polytope) space-filling [tessellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation)s (or [honeycombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeycomb_(geometry))).

ordered field is a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) together with a [total order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_order)ing of its elements that is compatible with the field operations.

Ordered geometry is a form of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) featuring the concept of intermediacy (or concept of parallelism does not form an [equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation) on lines.

ordered ring is a (usually [commutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_ring)) [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)) R with a [total order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_order) ≤ such that for all a, b, and c in R: as either b or −b is positive, a must be nonnegative.
orientation of a real vector space or simply orientation of a vector space is the arbitrary choice of which ordered [bases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_(mathematics)) are from point to point.

orientation, attitude, bearing or angular position of an object – such as a [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)), [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) or [rigid body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_body) – is the [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation) needed to move the object from a reference placement to its current placement.

orientation of a building refers to the direction in which it is constructed and laid out, taking account of its planned purpose and ease of use for its occupants, its relation to the path of the sun and other aspects of its environment.

orthant The nonnegative orthant is the generalization of the first [quadrant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrant_(plane_geometry)) to n-dimensions and is important in many [constrained optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constrained_optimization) problems.

orthologic if the [perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular)s from the [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)) of one of them to the corresponding sides of the other are [concurrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concurrent_lines) (i.e., they [intersect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line–line_intersection) at a single [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry))).
orthonormal frame is a tool for studying the structure of a [differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold) equipped with a metric.

osculant or tacinvariant or tact invariant is an invariant of a [hypersurface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersurface) that vanishes if the hypersurface touches itself, or an invariant of several hypersurfaces that [osculate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osculation), meaning that they have a common point where they meet to unusually high order.

definition: osculating plane is a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)) in a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) or [affine space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_space) which meets a [submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submanifold) at a [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) in such a way as to have a second order of [contact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_(mathematics)) at the point.

Osserman manifold is a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) in which the [characteristic polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_polynomial) of the [Jacobi operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_operator) of [unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_vector) [tangent vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_vector)s is a constant on the unit [tangent bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_bundle).
Ostomachion, also known as () or syntomachion, is a mathematical treatise attributed to [Archimedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes).

Oswald Veblen Prize in Geometry is an award granted by the [American Mathematical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Mathematical_Society) for notable research in [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) or [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology).

Otfried Cheong (; formerly Otfried Schwarzkopf) is a German [computational geometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry) working in [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea) at [KAIST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KAIST).

outermorphism of a [linear function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map) between [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)s is a natural extension of the map to arbitrary [multivector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivector)s.
ovoid is a sphere like pointset (surface) in a projective space of dimension .
ovoid O of a (finite) [polar space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_space) of rank r is a set of points, such that every subspace of rank points.

p-adic Hodge theory is a theory that provides a way to classify and study [p-adic Galois representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_representation) of [characteristic 0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_(algebra)) [local field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field)s Co.

-curvature is an invariant of a [connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_(mathematics)) on a [coherent sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf) for [schemes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) of characteristic {{math|p , Compositio Mathematica, 140.1 (Jan 2004): 145–164.

Pachner moves, named after Udo Pachner, are ways of replacing a [triangulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulation_(topology)) of a [piecewise linear manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piecewise_linear_manifold) by a different triangulation of a [homeomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism) manifold.

definition: packing dimension is one of a number of concepts that can be used to define the [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension) of a [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset) of a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space).
Paden–Kahan subproblems are a set of solved geometric problems which occur frequently in [inverse kinematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_kinematics) of common robotic manipulators.

pair of pants is a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(topology)) which is [homeomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphic) to the three-holed [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere).

Paneitz operator is a fourth-order [differential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_operator) defined on a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) of dimension n.

paper bag problem or teabag problem is to calculate the maximum possible inflated volume of an initially flat sealed rectangular bag which has the same shape as a [cushion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cushion) or [pillow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillow), made out of two pieces of material which can bend but not stretch.

Pappus chain is a ring of [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle)s between two [tangent circles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_circles) investigated by [Pappus of Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pappus_of_Alexandria) in the 3rd century [AD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AD).

Pappus configuration is a [configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Configuration_(geometry)) of nine points and nine lines in the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane), with three points per line and three lines through each point.

Pappus's area theorem describes the relationship between the areas of three [parallelogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallelogram)s attached to three sides of an arbitrary [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle).

Pappus's centroid theorem (also known as the Guldinus theorem, Pappus–Guldinus theorem or Pappus's theorem) is either of two related [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem)s dealing with the [surface area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_area)s and [volume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume)s of [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_of_revolution)s and [solid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_of_revolution)s of revolution.

parabolic geometry is a [homogeneous space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_space) G/P which is the quotient of a [semisimple Lie group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_group) G by a [parabolic subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borel_subgroup) P.
parabolic Hausdorff dimension is a restricted version of the genuine [Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension).
parabolic point when the [Gaussian curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_curvature) is zero.

paraboloid is a [quadric surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadric_surface) that has exactly one [axis of symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axial_symmetry) and no [center of symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_symmetry).
paradoxical set is a set that has a paradoxical decomposition.

parallel lines are [coplanar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coplanar) infinite straight [lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)) that do not [intersect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersecting_lines) at any point.

Parallel Coordinates plots are a common method of visualizing [high-dimensional datasets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_data) to analyze multivariate data having multiple variables, or attributes.

parallel curve of a given (progenitor) [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve) is the [envelope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(mathematics)) of a family of [congruent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_(geometry)) (equal-radius) [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle)s centered on the curve.

parallel postulate is the fifth postulate in [Euclid's Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements) and a distinctive [axiom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom) in [Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry).

paravector is used for the combination of a scalar and a vector in any [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra), known as [geometric algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_algebra) among physicists.

partial linear space (also semilinear or near-linear space) is a basic [incidence structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_structure) in the field of incidence geometry, that carries slightly less structure than a [linear space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_space_(geometry)).

Pascal's theorem (also known as the hexagrammum mysticum theorem, [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin) for mystical [hexagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexagram)) states that if six arbitrary points are chosen on a [conic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conic_section) (which may be an [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse), [parabola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parabola) or [hyperbola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbola) in an appropriate [affine plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_plane)) and joined by line segments in any order to form a [hexagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexagon), then the three pairs of opposite [sides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(geometry)) of the hexagon ([extended](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_side) if necessary) meet at three points which lie on a straight line, called the Pascal line of the hexagon.
Path integration is the method thought to be used by animals for [dead reckoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_reckoning).

Pauling's rules are five rules published by [Linus Pauling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Pauling) in 1929 for [predicting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_structure_prediction) and rationalizing the [crystal structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_structure)s of [ionic compound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_compound)s.

PDIFF, for piecewise differentiable, is the [category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) of [piecewise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piecewise)-[smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoothness) [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s and piecewise-smooth [maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) between them.

pencil is a family of geometric objects with a common property, for example the set of [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry))s that pass through a given point in a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)), or the set of [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle)s that pass through two given points in a plane.

Pendent is an adjective that describes the condition of hanging, either literally, or figuratively, [[File:Santa Maria del Fiore.jpg|thumb|left|The dome of [Florence Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Cathedral) (Santa Maria del Fiore), constructed in segments.
Penrose tiling is an example of an [aperiodic tiling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aperiodic_tiling).

Penrose transform, introduced by , is a complex analogue of the [Radon transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radon_transform) that relates massless fields on spacetime, or more precisely the space of solutions to massless [field equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_equation)s, to [sheaf cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_cohomology) groups on [complex projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_projective_space).

pentagram map is a [[Dynamical system#Discrete dynamical system|discrete dynamical system]] acting on [polygons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygons) in the [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane).

perfect obstruction theory for X consists of: # a [perfect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_complex) two-term complex is a smooth local complete intersection then the perfect obstruction theory is the cotangent complex (which is the same as the truncated cotangent complex).
perfect rectangle is a [rectangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangle) that can be divided into [square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square)s of different sizes.

perimeter is the [length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length) of a closed [boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary_(topology)) that encompasses, surrounds, or outlines either a [two-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_space) [shape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape) or a [one-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-dimensional_space) [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(graphics)).
periodic table of mathematical shapes is the popular name given to a project to classify [Fano varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano_varieties).

Perles configuration is a system of nine points and nine lines in the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane) for which every combinatorially equivalent realization has at least one [irrational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrational_number) as one of its coordinates.

permutation graph is a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) whose [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(graph_theory)) represent the elements of a [permutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation), and whose edges represent pairs of elements that are [reversed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversion_(discrete_mathematics)) by the permutation.
Geological perspective correlation is a theory in [geology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology) describing geometrical regularities in the layering of sediments.

Petersen–Morley theorem states that, if , , are three general [skew lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skew_lines) in space, if , , are the lines of shortest distance respectively for the pairs , and , and if , and are the lines of shortest distance respectively for the pairs , and , then there is a single line meeting at right angles all of , , and .

Petrov classification (also known as Petrov–Pirani–Penrose classification) describes the possible algebraic [symmetries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry) of the [Weyl tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_tensor) at each [[Spacetime#Basic concepts|event]] in a [Lorentzian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentzian_manifold).

phase response is the relationship between the [phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_(waves)) of a [sinusoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_wave)al input and the output [signal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_(information_theory)) passing through any device that accepts input and produces an output signal, such as an [amplifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplifier) or a [filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filter_(signal_processing)).

phase-space formulation is a formulation of [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics) that places the [position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Position_(vector)) and [momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum) variables on equal footing in [phase space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_space).

Philo line is a [line segment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_segment) defined from an [angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle) and a [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) inside the angle as the shortest line segment through the point that has its endpoints on the two sides of the angle.

Picard group of a [ringed space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ringed_space) X, denoted by Pic(X), is the group of [isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism) classes of [invertible sheaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invertible_sheaves) (or [line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_bundle)s) on X, with the [group operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_operation) being [tensor product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product).

Picard horn, also called the Picard topology or Picard model, is one of the oldest known [hyperbolic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_geometry) [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s, first described by [Émile Picard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émile_Picard) }} [[Category:3-manifolds]] [[Category:Hyperbolic manifolds]] [[Category:Physical cosmology]] 6cy84sqi89if9yus7hs6csyzwj6mx3b

piecewise algebraic space is a generalization of a [semialgebraic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semialgebraic_set), introduced by [Maxim Kontsevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxim_Kontsevich) and [Yan Soibelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan_Soibelman).
piecewise linear manifold (PL manifold) is a [topological manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_manifold) together with a piecewise linear structure on it.

pinhole camera model describes the mathematical relationship between the [coordinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate)s of a point in [three-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space) and its [projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_projection) onto the [image plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_plane) of an [pinhole camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinhole_camera), where the camera [aperture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aperture) is described as a point and no lenses are used to focus light.

pinwheel tilings are [non-periodic tilings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aperiodic_tiling) defined by [Charles Radin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Radin) and based on a construction due to [[John H.

Pitteway triangulation is a [point set triangulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_set_triangulation) in which the [nearest neighbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search) of any point p within the triangulation is one of the vertices of the triangle containing p.

planar process is a [manufacturing process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_device_fabrication) used in the [semiconductor industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_industry) to build individual components of a [transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor), and in turn, connect those transistors together.

Planar projections are the subset of [3D graphical projections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_projection) constructed by [linearly mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_map) points in [three-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space) to points on a [two-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional) projection plane.

plane is a [two-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_space) or [flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_space) [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)) that extends indefinitely.

plane at infinity is the [hyperplane at infinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperplane_at_infinity) of a three dimensional [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) or to any [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) contained in the hyperplane at infinity of any projective space of higher dimension.

plane curve is a [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve) in a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) that may be a [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)), an [affine plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_plane) or a [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane).
plane mirror is a [mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror) with a flat ([planar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics))) reflective surface.
plane of rotation is an abstract object used to describe or visualize [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation_(mathematics))s in space.

plane symmetry is a symmetry of a pattern in the [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane): that is, a transformation of the plane that carries any direction lines to lines and preserves many different distances.

plane wave is a special case of a [wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_(physics)) or [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(physics)): a physical quantity whose value, at any given moment, is constant through any plane that is perpendicular to a fixed direction in space.

Plane-based geometric algebra is an application of [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra) to modelling planes, lines, points, and [rigid transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigid_transformation)s.

Platonic solid is a [convex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_polyhedron), [regular polyhedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_polyhedron) in [three-dimensional Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space).
pleated surface is roughly a surface that may have simple folds but is not crumpled in more complicated ways.

plumb bob, plumb bob level, or plummet, is a weight, usually with a pointed tip on the bottom, suspended from a string and used as a [vertical direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_direction) as a reference line, or plumb-line.

Plücker coordinates, introduced by [Julius Plücker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Plücker) in the 19th century, are a way to assign six [homogeneous coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homogeneous_coordinates) to each [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(mathematics)) in [projective 3-space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space), .
Plücker's conoid is a [ruled surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruled_surface) named after the German mathematician [Julius Plücker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Plücker).
Pohlke's theorem is the fundamental theorem of [axonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axonometry).

Poincaré half-plane model is a way of representing the [hyperbolic plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_plane) using points in the familiar [Euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_plane).

point-set registration, also known as point-cloud registration or scan matching, is the process of finding a spatial [transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_transformation) (e.g., [scaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scaling_(geometry)), [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation) and [translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_(geometry))) that aligns two [point cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_cloud)s.

points of the compass are a set of horizontal, [radially](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius) arrayed compass directions (or [[Azimuth#In navigation|azimuths]]) used in [navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation) and [cartography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartography).

Poisson manifold is a [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold) endowed with a Poisson structure.

prescribed Ricci curvature problem is as follows: given a [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold) M and a symmetric 2-tensor h, construct a [metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric) on M whose [Ricci curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricci_curvature) [tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor) equals h.

prescribed scalar curvature problem is as follows: given a [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_manifold), [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold) M and a smooth, real-valued function ƒ on M, construct a [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_metric) on M whose [scalar curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_curvature) equals ƒ.

presymplectic form is a [geometric structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_structure) on [differentiable manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold).

Lasker–Noether theorem states that every [Noetherian ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) is a Lasker ring, which means that every ideal can be decomposed as an intersection, called primary decomposition, of finitely many [primary ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_ideal)s (which are related to, but not quite the same as, powers of [prime ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_ideal)s).

prime decomposition theorem for 3-manifolds states that every [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space), [orientable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientability) [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold) is the [connected sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connected_sum) of a unique ([up to](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Up_to) [homeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism)) finite collection of [prime 3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_manifold)s.

prime geodesic on a [hyperbolic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_geometry) [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)) is a primitive [closed geodesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_geodesic): one whose parametrization is not obtained by going repeatedly around a shorter closed geodesic.

principal axis is a certain line in a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) associated with a [ellipsoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipsoid) or [hyperboloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperboloid), generalizing the major and minor [axes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_symmetry) of an [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse) or [hyperbola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbola).

principal curvatures at a given point of a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)) are the maximum and minimum values of the [curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature) as expressed by the [eigenvalues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues) of the [shape operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape_operator) at that point.

priority search tree is a tree [data structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure) for storing points in two dimensions.

quantum differential calculus or noncommutative differential structure on an algebra is the algebra product.

quarter hypercubic honeycomb (or quarter n-cubic honeycomb) is a dimensional infinite series of [honeycomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeycomb_(geometry))s, based on the [hypercube honeycomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercube_honeycomb).

quasi-isometry is a [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) between two [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space)s that respects large-scale geometry of these spaces and ignores their small-scale details.
quasi-triangulation is a subdivision of a geometric object into simplices, where vertices are not points but arbitrary sloped line segments.

quasisymmetric [homeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism) between metric spaces is a map that generalizes [bi-Lipschitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipschitz_function) maps.

Rabatment of the rectangle is a compositional technique used as an aid for the placement of objects or the division of space within a rectangular frame, or as an aid for the study of art.

Rabattement (also rabatment) is a [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation_around_a_fixed_axis) of a planar object around a folding line (using the line like a [hinge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinge)) in order to align the object with another plane.

Radio navigation or radionavigation is the application of [radio wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_wave)s to [determine a position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geolocalization) of an object on the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth), either the vessel or an obstruction.

Ragsdale conjecture is a [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) that concerns the possible arrangements of real [algebraic curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curves) embedded in the [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane).
Rail directions are used to describe train directions on rail systems.

Ralph Brown (1928 – 2013) was an English sculptor who came to national prominence in the late 1950s with his large-scale bronze Meat Porters, commissioned for Harlow New Town, Essex and is known for his sensual, figurative sculptures.

Ramer–Douglas–Peucker algorithm, also known as the Douglas–Peucker algorithm and iterative end-point fit algorithm, is an algorithm that [decimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimation_(signal_processing)) a curve composed of line segments to a similar curve with fewer points.

Random sample consensus (RANSAC) is an [iterative method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterative_method) to estimate parameters of a mathematical model from a set of observed data that contains [outliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outliers), when outliers do not affect the values of the estimates.
Range Query Tree, or RQT, is a term for referring to a data structure that is used for performing range queries and updates on an underlying array, which is treated as the leaves of the tree.
range searching problem consists of processing a set S of objects, in order to determine which objects from S intersect with a query object, called the range.

raster graphic, raster image, or simply raster is a [digital image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_image) made up of a rectangular grid of tiny colored (usually square) so-called [pixel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel)s.
rational map or rational mapping is a kind of [partial function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_function) between [algebraic varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_varieties).

rational normal curve is a smooth, [rational curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_curve) of [degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_an_algebraic_variety) in [projective n-space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) of degree is a rational normal curve.
rational point of an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) is a point whose coordinates belong to a given [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)).

rational surface is a surface [birationally equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birational_geometry) to the [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane), or in other words a [rational variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_variety) of dimension two.

rational variety is an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety), over a given [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K, which is [birationally equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birationally_equivalent) to a [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) of some dimension over K.

Rauch comparison theorem, named after [Harry Rauch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Rauch), who proved it in 1951, is a fundamental result which relates the [sectional curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sectional_curvature) of a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) to the rate at which [geodesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic)s spread apart.

real number is a [number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number) that can be used to [measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurement) a [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_variable) one-[dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)al [quantity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantity) such as a [length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length), [duration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time) or [temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature).

real RAM ([random-access machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random-access_machine)) is a mathematical [model of a computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_of_computation) that can compute with exact [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)s instead of the binary [fixed-point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed-point_arithmetic) or [floating-point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic) numbers used by most actual computers.

real-root isolation of a [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) consist of producing disjoint [interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(mathematics))s of the [real line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_line), which contain each one (and only one) real [root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_function) of the polynomial, and, together, contain all the real roots of the polynomial.

Rectangle packing is a [packing problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_problem) where the objective is to determine whether a given set of small rectangles can be placed inside a given large polygon, such that no two small rectangles overlap.

rectilinear Steiner tree problem, minimum rectilinear Steiner tree problem (MRST), or rectilinear Steiner minimum tree problem (RSMT) is a variant of the geometric [Steiner tree problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_tree_problem) in the plane, in which the [Euclidean distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance) is replaced with the [rectilinear distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectilinear_distance).
