regular chain is a particular kind of triangular set of [multivariate polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_polynomial)s over a field, where a triangular set is a finite sequence of polynomials such that each one contains at least one more indeterminate than the preceding one.

regular local ring is a [Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noetherian_ring) [local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring) having the property that the minimal number of [generators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_set_of_a_module) of its [maximal ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximal_ideal) is equal to its [Krull dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krull_dimension).

regular scheme is a [locally Noetherian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_Noetherian_scheme) [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) whose [local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring)s are [regular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_local_ring) everywhere.
regular semi-algebraic system is a particular kind of triangular system of multivariate polynomials over a real closed field.

regulus R is a set of [skew lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skew_lines), every point of which is on a [transversal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transversal_(combinatorics)) which intersects an element of R only once, and such that every point on a transversal lies on a line of R.
Reilly formula is an important [identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_(mathematics)), discovered by Robert Reilly in 1977.
relative contact homology is an invariant of spaces together with a chosen subspace.
relative cycle is a type of [algebraic cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_cycle) on a [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)).
relative effective Cartier divisor is roughly a family of [effective Cartier divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_Cartier_divisor)s.

reprojection error is a geometric error corresponding to the image distance between a projected point and a measured one.

Research in Number Theory is a [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed) [mathematics journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_journal) covering [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory) and [arithmetic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_geometry).
residue field is a basic construction in [commutative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_algebra).

Reuleaux tetrahedron is the intersection of four [balls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_(mathematics)) of [radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius) s centered at the [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)) of a regular [tetrahedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedron) with side length s.

Reye configuration, introduced by , is a [configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Configuration_(geometry)) of 12 [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) and 16 [lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)).

ribbon (or strip) is the combination of a [smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoothness) [space curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_curve) and its corresponding [normal vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_vector).
Ribet's theorem (earlier called the epsilon conjecture or ε-conjecture) is part of [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory).

Ricci decomposition is a way of breaking up the [Riemann curvature tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_tensor) of a [Riemannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) or [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Riemannian_manifold) into pieces with special algebraic properties.

Ricci flow ( , ), sometimes also referred to as Hamilton's Ricci flow, is a certain [partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equation) for a [Riemannian metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold).

Riemann curvature tensor or Riemann–Christoffel tensor (after [Bernhard Riemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_Riemann) and [Elwin Bruno Christoffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elwin_Bruno_Christoffel)) is the most common way used to express the [curvature of Riemannian manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature_of_Riemannian_manifolds).

Riemann's minimal surface is a one-parameter family of [minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface)s described by [Bernhard Riemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_Riemann) in a posthumous paper published in 1867.

Riemannian connection on a [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(topology)) or [Riemannian 2-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) refers to several intrinsic geometric structures discovered by [Tullio Levi-Civita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tullio_Levi-Civita), [Élie Cartan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Élie_Cartan) and [Hermann Weyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Weyl) in the early part of the twentieth century: [parallel transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_transport), [covariant derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_derivative) and [connection form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_form).

Riemannian manifold (or Riemann space) is a [geometric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_space) on which many geometric notions such as distance, angles, length, volume, and curvature are defined.

definition: Riemannian submersion is a [submersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submersion_(mathematics)) from one [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) to another that respects the metrics, meaning that it is an [orthogonal projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal_projection) on tangent spaces.

Riemann–Roch theorem for smooth manifolds is a version of results such as the [Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch_theorem) or [Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch_theorem) (GRR) without a hypothesis making the [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold)s involved carry a [complex structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_manifold).
right circular cylinder is a [cylinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylinder) whose [generatrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generatrices) are perpendicular to the bases.

right conoid is a [ruled surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruled_surface) generated by a family of [straight line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_line)s that all intersect [perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular)ly to a fixed straight line, called the axis of the right [conoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conoid).

right triangle or right-angled triangle, sometimes called an orthogonal triangle or rectangular triangle, is a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) in which two [sides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(geometry)) are [perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular), forming a [right angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_angle) ( [turn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_(unit)) or 90 [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_(angle))).

right-hand rule is a [convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_(norm)) and a [mnemonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnemonic) utilized to define the [orientation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientation_(vector_space)) of [axes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_coordinate_system) in [three-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space) and to determine the [direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direction_(geometry)) of the [cross product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_product) of two [vectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector), as well as to establish the direction of the force on a [current-carrying conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_current) in a [magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_field).
rigid cohomology is a [-adic cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_cohomology) theory introduced by [Pierre Berthelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Berthelot) in 1986.

ring is an ambiguous term referring either to a simple [[wikt:cyclic#Chemistry|cycle]] of atoms and bonds in a molecule or to a connected set of atoms and bonds in which every atom and bond is a member of a cycle (also called a ring system).

ring flip (also known as a ring inversion or ring reversal) is the interconversion of cyclic [conformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformational_isomerism)s that have equivalent [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(chemistry)) shapes (e.g., from a chair conformer to another chair conformer) that results in the exchange of nonequivalent [substituent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substituent) positions.

Robbins pentagon is a [cyclic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_polygon) [pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon) whose side lengths and area are all [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number)s.
Robert Ernest Clatworthy [RA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Academician) (31 January 1928 – 15 or 16 March 2015) was a British sculptor and teacher of art.

Robert Connelly (born July 15, 1942) is a mathematician specializing in [discrete geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_geometry) and [rigidity theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigidity_theory_(structural)).

Robert Lawlor (August 11, 1938 – November 29, 2022) was an American [mythographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mythographer), [symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbol)ogist and [New Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Age) author of several books.

definition: geometric nonrobustness is a problem wherein branching decisions in [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry) algorithms are based on approximate numerical computations, leading to various forms of unreliability including ill-formed output and software failure through crashing or infinite loops.

Roger Long (1680 – 16 December 1770) was an English [astronomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomer), and Master of [Pembroke College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembroke_College,_Cambridge), [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge) between 1733 and 1770.
categories: Lowndean Professors of Astronomy and Geometry

definition: root system is a configuration of [vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)s in a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) satisfying certain geometrical properties.

Rosati involution, named after [Carlo Rosati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Rosati), is an involution of the rational [endomorphism ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endomorphism_ring) of an [abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety) induced by a [[Abelian_variety#Polarisations|polarisation]].

Rota's basis conjecture is an unproven [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) concerning rearrangements of [bases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_(linear_algebra)), named after [Gian-Carlo Rota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gian-Carlo_Rota).

rotating calipers is an [algorithm design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm_design) technique that can be used to solve optimization problems including finding the width or [diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diameter_(computational_geometry)) of a set of points.
Rotation, also known as rotational motion or rotary motion, is the [movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_(physics)) of an object that leaves at least one point unchanged.

definition: rotations about a fixed point in [four-dimensional Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-dimensional_space) is denoted SO(4).

rotor is an object in the [geometric algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_algebra) (also called [Clifford algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_algebra)) of a [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space) that represents a [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation_(mathematics)) about the [origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_(mathematics)).
round function is a [scalar function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_function) 18.[http://citeseer.ist.psu.edu/287481.html].
Roundness is the measure of how closely the shape of an object approaches that of a mathematically perfect [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle).

rule of marteloio is a [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages) technique of [navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation)al computation that uses [compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass) direction, [distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance) and a simple [trigonometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry) table known as the toleta de marteloio.
ruled (also called a scroll) if through every [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) of , there is a [straight line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_line) that lies on .
ruling grade is the steepest [grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_(slope)) on the [rail line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_line) between two locations.

Ruppeiner geometry is thermodynamic geometry (a type of [information geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_geometry)) using the language of [Riemannian geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_geometry) to study [thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermodynamics).

Rytz’s axis construction is a basic method of [descriptive geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descriptive_geometry) to find the axes, the [semi-major axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-major_axis) and [semi-minor axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-minor_axis) and the vertices of an [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse), starting from two [conjugated half-diameters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_diameters).

Saccheri quadrilateral is a [quadrilateral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrilateral) with two equal [sides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(geometry)) [perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular) to the [base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_(geometry)).
Saccheri–Legendre theorem states that the sum of the angles in a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) is at most 180°.

Sacral architecture (also known as sacred architecture or religious architecture) is a [religious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion) [architectural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture) practice concerned with the design and construction of [places of worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_of_worship) or sacred or intentional space, such as [churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_architecture), [[Mosque#Architecture|mosques]], [stupa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stupa)s, [synagogues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synagogue_architecture), and [temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple)s.

definition: Sangaku or san gaku () are Japanese [geometrical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry) problems or theorems on wooden tablets which were placed as offerings at [Shinto shrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinto_shrine)s or [Buddhist temples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_temples_in_Japan) during the [Edo period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_period) by members of all social classes.

Santaló's formula describes how to integrate a function on the unit [sphere bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_bundle) of a [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) by first integrating along every [geodesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic) separately and then over the space of all geodesics.

Savilian Professor of Geometry was established at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford) in 1619.
scalar curvature (or the Ricci scalar) is a measure of the [curvature of a Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature_of_Riemannian_manifolds).

schema for horizontal dials is a set of instructions used to construct horizontal [sundial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundial)s using [compass and straightedge construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_and_straightedge_construction) techniques, which were widely used in Europe from the late fifteenth century to the late nineteenth century.

Schlessinger's theorem is a theorem in [deformation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_theory) introduced by that gives conditions for a [functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functor) of [artinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artinian_ring) [local ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ring)s to be pro-representable, refining an earlier theorem of [Grothendieck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grothendieck).

Schläfli double six is a [configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Configuration_(geometry)) of 30 points and 12 lines in three-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space), introduced by [Ludwig Schläfli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Schläfli) in 1858.

Schoenflies problem or Schoenflies theorem, of [geometric topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_topology) is a sharpening of the [Jordan curve theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_curve_theorem) by [Arthur Schoenflies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Moritz_Schoenflies).

Schoen–Yau conjecture is a disproved conjecture in [hyperbolic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_geometry), named after the [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician)s [Richard Schoen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Schoen) and [Shing-Tung Yau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shing-Tung_Yau).

Schouten–Nijenhuis bracket, also known as the Schouten bracket, is a type of [graded Lie bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graded_Lie_algebra) defined on [multivector fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyvector_Field) on a [smooth manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_manifold) extending the [Lie bracket of vector fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_bracket_of_vector_fields).
Schur's lemma is a result that says, heuristically, whenever certain curvatures are pointwise constant then they are forced to be globally constant.

Schur's theorem is any of several [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem)s of the [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) [Issai Schur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issai_Schur).

Schwarz minimal surfaces are [periodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triply_periodic_minimal_surface) [minimal surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface)s originally described by [Hermann Schwarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Schwarz).

Schwarz triangle, named after [Hermann Schwarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Schwarz), is a [spherical triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_triangle) that can be used to [tile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation) a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) ([spherical tiling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_tiling)), possibly overlapping, through reflections in its edges.

definition: Schwarz triangle function or Schwarz s-function is a function that [conformally maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_mapping) the [upper half plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_half_plane) to a triangle in the upper half plane having lines or circular arcs for edges.

Schwarzian derivative is an operator similar to the [derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative) which is invariant under [Möbius transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Möbius_transformation)s.

Schwarz–Ahlfors–Pick theorem is an extension of the [Schwarz lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarz_lemma) for [hyperbolic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_geometry), such as the [Poincaré half-plane model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincaré_half-plane_model).

screw axis (helical axis or twist axis) is a line that is simultaneously the [axis of rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_of_rotation) and the line along which [translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_(geometry)) of a body occurs.

secant plane is a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) containing a nontrivial [section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(geometry)) of a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) or an [ellipsoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipsoid), or such a plane that a sphere is projected onto.

second [covariant derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariant_derivative), or the second order covariant derivative, of a vector field is the derivative of its derivative with respect to another two [tangent vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_vector) fields.

second fundamental form (or shape tensor) is a [quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form) on the [tangent plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_plane) of a [smooth surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry_of_surfaces) in the three-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space), usually denoted by .

second moment of area, or second area moment, or quadratic moment of area and also known as the area moment of inertia, is a geometrical property of an [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area) which reflects how its points are distributed with regard to an arbitrary axis.
secondary vector bundle structure refers to the natural [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle) structure .
Section formula is a formula used to find the ratio in which a line segment is divided by a point internally or externally.
sectional curvature is one of the ways to describe the [curvature of Riemannian manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature_of_Riemannian_manifolds).
seesaw theorem, or seesaw principle, says roughly that a limit of trivial line bundles over [complete varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_variety) is a trivial line bundle.

Segre embedding is a map used in [projective geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_geometry) to consider the [cartesian product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product) of two [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space)s as a [projective variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_variety).

Seiberg–Witten flow is a [gradient flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_flow) described by the [Seiberg–Witten equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiberg–Witten_equations), hence a method to describe a [gradient descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent) of the Seiberg–Witten action functional.

Seiberg–Witten moduli space (short SW moduli space, also monopole moduli space) is the [moduli space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moduli_space) of the [Seiberg–Witten equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiberg–Witten_equations), hence the space of its solutions up to gauge.
Seifert fiber space is a [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold) together with a decomposition as a disjoint union of circles.

Seifert–Weber space (introduced by [Herbert Seifert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Seifert) and Constantin Weber) is a [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_manifold) [hyperbolic 3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_3-manifold).
Seked (or seqed) is an ancient Egyptian term describing the inclination of the triangular faces of a right pyramid.

self-avoiding walk (SAW) is a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence) of moves on a [lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_(group)) (a [lattice path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_path)) that does not visit the same point more than once.

Semi-global matching (SGM) is a [computer vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_vision) [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) for the estimation of a dense [disparity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binocular_disparity) map from a [rectified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_rectification) [stereo image pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoscopy), introduced in 2005 by Heiko Hirschmüller while working at the [German Aerospace Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Aerospace_Center).

semi-orthogonal matrix is a non-[square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_matrix) [matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) with [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) entries where: if the number of columns exceeds the number of rows, then the rows are [orthonormal vectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthonormal_vectors); but if the number of rows exceeds the number of columns, then the columns are orthonormal vectors.

semi-simplicity is a widespread concept in disciplines such as [linear algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_algebra), [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra), [representation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_theory), [category theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory), and [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry).

k-semi-Yao graph (k-SYG) of a set of n objects P is a geometric proximity graph, which was first described to present a [kinetic data structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinetic_data_structure) for maintenance of [all the nearest neighbors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_graph) on moving objects.

basic semialgebraic set is a set defined by polynomial equalities and polynomial inequalities, and a semialgebraic set is a [finite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_set) [union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(set_theory)) of basic semialgebraic sets.
semialgebraic space is a space which is locally [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism) to a [semialgebraic set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semialgebraic_set).

arbelos (grey region)]] An [arbelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbelos) is a region in the [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) bounded by three semicircles connected at their endpoints, all on the same side of a [straight line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_line) (the baseline) that contains their [diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diameter)s.

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a subfield of [mathematical programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_programming) concerned with the optimization of a linear [objective function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objective_function) (a user-specified function that the user wants to minimize or maximize) over the intersection of the [cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_(linear_algebra)) of [[Positive-definite matrix#Negative-definite, semidefinite and indefinite matrices|positive semidefinite]] [matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics)) with an [affine space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_space), i.e., a [spectrahedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrahedron).

semiorthogonal decomposition is a way to divide a [triangulated category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulated_category) into simpler pieces.
semiperimeter of a [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon) is half its [perimeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perimeter).

semistable abelian variety is an [abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_variety) defined over a [global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_field) or [local field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field), which is characterized by how it reduces at the primes of the field.
Semplicità is a [sans-serif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sans-serif) [typeface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typeface) of the [[Sans-serif#Geometric|geometric style]].

definition: Serre duality is a [duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duality_(mathematics)) for the [coherent sheaf cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_sheaf_cohomology) of algebraic varieties, proved by [Jean-Pierre Serre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Serre).

Serre's theorem on affineness (also called Serre's cohomological characterization of affineness or Serre's criterion on affineness) is a theorem due to [Jean-Pierre Serre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Serre) which gives sufficient conditions for a [scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheme_(mathematics)) to be [affine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_ring), stated in terms of [sheaf cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_cohomology).

Severi–Brauer variety over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)) K is an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) V which becomes [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphic) to a [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space) over an [algebraic closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_closure) of K.

shape is a [graphical representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics) of an object's form or its external boundary, outline, or external [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_(mathematics)).

definition: Shape moiré is one type of [moiré pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moiré_pattern)s demonstrating the phenomenon of moiré magnification.

Sharafutdinov's retraction is a construction that gives a [retraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deformation_retract) of an open non-negatively curved [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) onto its soul.

sheaf (: sheaves) is a tool for systematically tracking data (such as [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics))s, [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group)s, [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics))s) attached to the [open set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set)s of a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) and defined locally with regard to them.

sheaf cohomology is the application of [homological algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_algebra) to analyze the [global section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_section)s of a [sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_(mathematics)) on a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space).
sheaf of planes is the set of all [planes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) that have the same common [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_(geometry)).

Shimura variety is a higher-dimensional analogue of a [modular curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_curve) that arises as a quotient [variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) of a [Hermitian symmetric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitian_symmetric_space) by a [congruence subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_subgroup) of a [reductive algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductive_group) defined over Q.

Siegel's lemma refers to bounds on the solutions of [linear equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_equation)s obtained by the construction of [auxiliary function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_function)s.

signature is an integer [invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_(mathematics)) which is defined for an oriented [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold) M of dimension [divisible by four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisible_by_four).
similarity system of triangles is a specific configuration involving a set of triangles.

Simons cone refers to a specific [minimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_surface) [hypersurface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersurface) in [Annals of Mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annals_of_Mathematics), 88 pp.

Simons formula (also known as the Simons identity, and in some variants as the Simons inequality) is a fundamental equation in the study of [minimal submanifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_submanifold)s.

simple polytope is a -dimensional [polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope) each of whose [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)) are adjacent to exactly [edges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(geometry)) (also [facets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facet_(geometry))).

simplex (plural: simplexes or simplices) is a generalization of the notion of a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) or [tetrahedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedron) to arbitrary [dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimensions).

simplicial complex is a structured [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) of [simplices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplex) (for example, [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry))s, [line segment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_segment)s, [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle)s, and their n-dimensional counterparts) such that all the [faces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_(geometry)) and intersections of the elements are also included in the set (see illustration).
simplicial depth is a measure of [central tendency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_tendency) determined by the [simplices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplex) that contain a given point.

simplicial polytope is a [polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytope) whose [facets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facet_(mathematics)) are all [simplices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplex).
Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a process where a computer constructs or updates a map of an unknown environment while simultaneously keeping track of an entity's location within it.

definition: sine wave, sinusoidal wave, or sinusoid (symbol: ∿) is a [periodic wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_function) whose [waveform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waveform) (shape) is the [trigonometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_function) [sine function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine).

sine-Gordon equation is a second-order [nonlinear partial differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_partial_differential_equation) for a function == See also == * [Josephson effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josephson_effect) * [Fluxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluxon) * [Shape waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape_waves) == References == == External links == * [http://eqworld.ipmnet.ru/en/solutions/npde/npde2106.pdf sine-Gordon equation] at EqWorld: The World of Mathematical Equations.
sine-triple-angle circle is one of many [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle)s that can be defined from a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle).

Sinistral and dextral, in some scientific fields, are the two types of [chirality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirality) ( ==See also== * [Dexter and sinister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dexter_and_sinister), as used in [heraldry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldry) * [Helicity (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicity_(disambiguation)) * [Jeremy (snail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_(snail)) * [Laterality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laterality) * [Left and right (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_and_right_(disambiguation)) * [Symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry) * [Terms of orientation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terms_of_orientation) == References == ==External links== [[Category:Chirality]] [[Category:Orientation
skirret is an archaic form of [chalk line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalk_line).

slam-dunk is a particular modification of a given [surgery diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehn_surgery) in the [3-sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-sphere) for a [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold).

sliver polygon, in the context of [Geographic Information System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_information_system)s (GIS), is a small [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon) found in [vector data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_graphics) that is an artifact of error rather than representing a real-world feature.

small cancellation theory studies groups given by [group presentations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presentation_of_a_group) satisfying small cancellation conditions, that is where defining relations have pg=PP1 Tilings of the plane, hyperbolic groups and small cancellation conditions.] Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society, vol.

smooth completion (or smooth compactification) of a [smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_scheme) [affine algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_algebraic_curve) X is a [complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_variety) smooth [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) which contains X as an open subset.
smooth projective planes are special [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane)s.
smooth topology is a certain [Grothendieck topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_topology) which is finer than [étale topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étale_topology).

Snellius–Pothenot problem is a [trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry) problem first described in the context of planar [surveying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveying) where known points are used to solve an unknown one.
Soddy line of a triangle is the line that goes through the centers of the two [Soddy circles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soddy_circles_of_a_triangle) of that triangle.

Soddy's hexlet is a chain of six [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere)s (shown in grey in Figure 1), each of which is [tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent) to both of its neighbors and also to three mutually tangent given spheres.

Solid geometry or stereometry is the [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) of [three-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_space) [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) (3D space).
Solid modeling (or solid modelling) is a consistent set of principles for mathematical and computer modeling of three-dimensional shapes [(solids)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_(mathematics)).

solid torus is the [solid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_(geometry)) formed by sweeping a [disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk_(mathematics)) around a [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle).

Solution of triangles () is the main [trigonometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry) problem of finding the characteristics of a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) (angles and lengths of sides), when some of these are known.

SOS-convex (or sum of squares convex) if its [Hessian matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hessian_matrix) H can be factored as H(x) = S Impressively, the same relation is valid for non-negative homogeneous polynomial in n variables and degree 2d that can be represented as sum of squares polynomials (See [Hilbert's seventeenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert's_seventeenth_problem)).

soul conjecture was proved by [Grigori Perelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grigori_Perelman), who established the more powerful fact that Sharafutdinov's retraction is a [Riemannian submersion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_submersion), and even a [submetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submetry).
South is one of the [cardinal direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_direction)s or [compass points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Points_of_the_compass).

space diagonal (also interior diagonal or body diagonal) of a [polyhedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyhedron) is a line connecting two [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry)) that are not on the same [face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_(geometry)).

space form is a [complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_space) [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) M of [constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant_curvature) [sectional curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sectional_curvature) K.
space group is the [symmetry group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_group) of a repeating pattern in space, usually in [three dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_dimensions).
space of directions at a point describes the directions of curves that start at the point.

space partitioning is the process of dividing an entire [space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space) (usually a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space)) into two or more [disjoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint_sets) [subset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subset)s (see also [partition of a set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_a_set)).

spacetime diagram is a graphical illustration of locations in space at various times, especially in the [special theory of relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_theory_of_relativity).

Spaltenstein variety is a variety given by the [fixed point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_point_(mathematics)) set of a nilpotent transformation on a [flag variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_variety).

spatial network (sometimes also [geometric graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_graph_theory)) is a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)) in which the [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(graph_theory)) or [edges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_(graph_theory)) are spatial elements associated with [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) objects, i.e., the nodes are located in a space equipped with a certain [metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_(mathematics)).
Special cases of Apollonius' problem are those in which at least one of the given circles is a point or line, i.e., is a circle of zero or infinite radius.

special conformal transformation is a [linear fractional transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_fractional_transformation) that is not an [affine transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_transformation).

special right triangle is a [right triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_triangle) with some notable feature that makes calculations on the [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) easier, or for which simple formulas exist.

spectral dimension is a [real-valued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) quantity that characterizes a [spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime) [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) and [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology).

Spectral geometry is a field in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) which concerns relationships between geometric structures of domains and [manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold)s and [spectra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_(functional_analysis)) of canonically defined [differential operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_operator)s.

spectral invariants are invariants defined for the group of Hamiltonian [diffeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffeomorphism)s of a [symplectic manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplectic_manifold), which is closed related to [Floer theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floer_homology) and Hofer geometry.

spectral space is a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) that is [homeomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphic) to the [spectrum of a commutative ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_of_a_ring).
spectral triple is a set of data which encodes a geometric phenomenon in an analytic way.

Sperner's lemma is a [combinatorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics) result on colorings of [triangulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulation_(geometry))s, [analogous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analogy) to the [Brouwer fixed point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brouwer_fixed_point_theorem), which is equivalent to it.
sphere packing is an arrangement of non-overlapping [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere)s within a containing space.

definition: Sphere packing in a cylinder is a three-dimensional [packing problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_problem) with the objective of packing a given number of identical [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere)s inside a [cylinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylinder) of specified diameter and length.

sphere-world was constructed by French mathematician [Henri Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Poincaré) who, while pursuing his argument for [conventionalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventionalism) (see [philosophy of space and time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy_of_space_and_time)), offered a [thought experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thought_experiment) about a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) with strange properties.

spherical 3-manifold M is a [3-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-manifold) of the form : When m is 1, the manifold is the [Poincaré homology sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincaré_homology_sphere).

spherical Bernstein's problem is a possible generalization of the original [Bernstein's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein's_problem) in the field of global [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry), first proposed by [Shiing-Shen Chern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiing-Shen_Chern) in 1969, and then later in 1970, during his plenary address at the [International Congress of Mathematicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Congress_of_Mathematicians) in [Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice).

spherical cap or spherical dome is a portion of a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) or of a [ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_(mathematics)) cut off by a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics)).

Spherical geometry or spherics () is the [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) of the two-[dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)al surface of a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere){{efn|In this context the word A statement that is equivalent to the parallel postulate is that there exists a triangle whose angles add up to 180°.

spherical image of a [[Curve#Length of a curve|unit-speed curve]] is given by taking the curve's [tangent vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_vector)s as points, all of which must lie on the [unit sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_sphere).
spherical sector, where is inclination (or elevation) and is azimuth (right).

spherical segment is the [solid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_(geometry)) defined by cutting a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere) or a [ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_(mathematics)) with a pair of [parallel planes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_(geometry)).
spherical shell (a [[Ball (mathematics)#Regions|ball shell]]) is a generalization of an [annulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annulus_(mathematics)) to three dimensions.
spherical variety is a G-variety with an open dense B-orbit.

spherical wedge or ungula is a portion of a [ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_(mathematics)) bounded by two plane [semidisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semidisk)s and a [spherical lune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_lune) (termed the wedge's base).

sphericity of a [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_theory) is a [graph invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_property) defined to be the smallest [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension) of [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) required to realize the graph as the [intersection graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_graph) of [congruent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_(geometry)) [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere)s.

Spherics (sometimes spelled sphaerics or sphaerica) is a term used in the [history of mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_mathematics) for historical works on [spherical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_geometry), ==References== [[Category:Spherical geometry]] [[Category:Classical geometry]] [[Category:Spherical astronomy]] [[Category:Ancient Greek mathematics]] oq6apkzy5ijkn5p03e4knjlsrx737sy

spidron is a continuous [flat geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_geometry) figure composed entirely of [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle)s, where, for every pair of joining triangles, each has a leg of the other as one of its legs, and neither has any point inside the interior of the other.
spin connection is a [connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_(vector_bundle)) on a [spinor bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinor_bundle).

spin geometry is the area of [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry) and [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) where objects like [spin manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_manifold)s and [Dirac operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_operator)s, and the various associated index theorems have come to play a fundamental role both in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) and in [mathematical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_physics).

spray is a [vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_field) H on the [tangent bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent_bundle) TM that encodes a [quasilinear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasiconvex_function) second order system of ordinary differential equations on the base manifold M.

Square packing is a [packing problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_problem) where the objective is to determine how many [congruent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_(geometry)) [square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square)s can be packed into some larger shape, often a square or circle.

square trisection is a type of [dissection problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissection_problem) which consists of [cutting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon_partition) a [square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square) into pieces that can be rearranged to form three identical squares.
Squaring the circle is a problem in [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry) first proposed in [Greek mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mathematics).
Squaring the square is the problem of [tiling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation) an integral square using only other integral squares.

Squigonometry or -trigonometry is a generalization of traditional [trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry) which replaces the [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle) and [Euclidean distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance) function with the [squircle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squircle) (shape intermediate between a [square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square) and circle) and [[Norm (mathematics)#p-norm|-norm]].

definition: stable normal bundle of a [differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold) is an invariant which encodes the stable normal (dually, tangential) data.

stable principal bundle is a generalisation of the notion of a [stable vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_vector_bundle) to the setting of [principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle)s.

stable vector bundle is a ([holomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_vector_bundle) or [algebraic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_vector_bundle)) [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle) that is stable in the sense of [geometric invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_invariant_theory).
(weakly) stable Yang–Mills (YM) connection is a Yang–Mills connection around which the Yang–Mills action functional is positively or even strictly positively curved.
(weakly) stable Yang–Mills–Higgs (YMH) pair is a Yang–Mills–Higgs pair around which the Yang–Mills–Higgs action functional is positively or even strictly positively curved.

stack or 2-sheaf is, roughly speaking, a [sheaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_(mathematics)) that takes values in [categories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_(mathematics)) rather than sets.

term: Stallings theorem about ends of groups
page: Stallings theorem about ends of groups

definition: standard conjectures about algebraic cycles are several [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture)s describing the relationship of [algebraic cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_cycle)s and [Weil cohomology theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_cohomology_theory).

standard monomial theory describes the sections of a [line bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_bundle) over a [generalized flag variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_flag_variety) or [Schubert variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert_variety) of a [reductive algebraic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductive_algebraic_group) by giving an explicit basis of elements called standard monomials.

star-shaped polygon is a [polygonal region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygonal_region) in the [euclidean plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) which is a [star domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_domain), that is, a polygon that contains a point from which the entire polygon boundary is [visible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visibility_polygon).

Steenrod's Problem (named after mathematician [Norman Steenrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Steenrod)) is a problem concerning the realisation of [homology class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homology_class)es by singular manifolds.

Stefan Langerman false Swarzberg is a Belgian [computer scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_scientist) and [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) whose research topics include [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry), [data structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_structure)s, and [recreational mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_mathematics).

Steiner chain is a set of circles, all of which are [tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent) to two given non-intersecting [circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle)s (blue and red in Figure 1), where is finite and each circle in the chain is tangent to the previous and next circles in the chain.

Steiner conic or more precisely Steiner's generation of a conic, named after the Swiss mathematician [Jakob Steiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakob_Steiner), is an alternative method to define a non-degenerate [projective conic section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadric_(projective_geometry)) in a [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane) over a [field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(mathematics)).

Steiner ellipse of a [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle) is the unique [circumellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumellipse) (an [ellipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipse) that touches the triangle at its [vertices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_(geometry))) whose center is the triangle's [centroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centroid).

Steiner point is a point that is not part of the input to a geometric optimization problem but is added during the solution of the problem, to create a better solution than would be possible from the original points alone.

Steiner tree problem, or minimum Steiner tree problem, named after [Jakob Steiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakob_Steiner), is an [umbrella term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umbrella_term) for a class of problems in [combinatorial optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial_optimization).

Steinerian of a [hypersurface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersurface), introduced by , is the [locus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locus_(mathematics)) of the [singular points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_point_of_an_algebraic_variety) of its [polar quadrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_classical_algebraic_geometry).

Steinmetz solid is the [solid body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_geometry) obtained as the [intersection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection) of two or three [cylinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylinder)s of equal radius [at right angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular).
Stencil jumping, at times called stencil walking, is an [algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm) to locate the grid element enclosing a given point for any structured mesh.

stereo cameras approach is a method of distilling a noisy [video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video) signal into a coherent data set that a computer can begin to process into actionable symbolic objects, or abstractions.

stereographic projection is a [perspective projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perspective_transform) of the [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere), through a specific [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) on the sphere (the pole or center of projection), onto a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) (the projection plane) [perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular) to the [diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diameter) through the point.

definition: steric tesseractic honeycomb is a uniform space-filling [tessellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation) (or [honeycomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeycomb_(geometry))) in Euclidean 4-space.

stericantic tesseractic honeycomb is a uniform space-filling [tessellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation) (or [honeycomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeycomb_(geometry))) in Euclidean 4-space.

steriruncic tesseractic honeycomb is a uniform space-filling [tessellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation) (or [honeycomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeycomb_(geometry))) in Euclidean 4-space.

steriruncicantic tesseractic honeycomb is a uniform space-filling [tessellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation) (or [honeycomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeycomb_(geometry))) in Euclidean 4-space.

Thurston's 24 questions are a set of [mathematical problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics) in [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry) posed by [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans) [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician) [William Thurston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Thurston) in his influential 1982 paper Three-dimensional manifolds, [Kleinian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kleinian_group)s and [hyperbolic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_geometry) published in the [Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulletin_of_the_American_Mathematical_Society).

Tic-tac-toe ([American English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English)), noughts and crosses ([Commonwealth English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_in_the_Commonwealth_of_Nations)), or Xs and Os ([Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_English) or [Irish English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiberno-English)) is a [paper-and-pencil game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper-and-pencil_game) for two players who take turns marking the spaces in a three-by-three grid, one with Xs and the other with Os.

Tienstra formula is used to solve the [resection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resection_(orientation)) problem in [surveying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveying), by which the location of a given point is determined by observations of angles to known landmarks from the unknown point.

metric envelope or tight span of a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space) M is an [injective metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injective_metric_space) into which M can be embedded.

time-varying phasors are used for analyzing narrow-band signals, whose signal bandwidths in the [frequency domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency_domain) are considerably smaller than the carrier frequency.

Tits metric is a [metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_(mathematics)) defined on the ideal boundary of an [Hadamard space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_space) (also called a [complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_metric_space) [CAT(0) space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAT(0)_space)).

Tomohiro Tachi (, born 1982) is a Japanese academic who studies [origami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origami) from an interdisciplinary perspective, combining approaches from the [mathematics of paper folding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_of_paper_folding), [structural rigidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_rigidity), [computational geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_geometry), [architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture), and [materials science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_science).
top-hat transform is an operation that extracts small elements and details from given [image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image)s.

topographic profile or topographic cut or elevation profile is a representation of the relief of the terrain that is obtained by [cutting transversely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(geometry)) the lines of a [topographic map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_map).
topological recursion is a recursive definition of invariants of spectral curves.

skeleton (or topological skeleton) of a [shape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape) is a thin version of that shape that is [equidistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistant) to its [boundaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary_(topology)).
Toponogov's theorem (named after [Victor Andreevich Toponogov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Andreevich_Toponogov)) is a triangle comparison theorem.

Torelli theorem, named after [Ruggiero Torelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruggiero_Torelli), is a classical result of [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry) over the [complex number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number_field), stating that a [[Algebraic curve#Singularities|non-singular]] projective [algebraic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_curve) ([compact Riemann surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Riemann_surface)) C is determined by its [Jacobian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_variety) J(C), when the latter is given in the form of a [principally polarized abelian variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principally_polarized_abelian_variety).
toric stack is a [stacky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(mathematics)) generalization of a [toric variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toric_variety).
toroid is a [surface of revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_of_revolution) with a hole in the middle.
toroidal embedding is an open embedding of algebraic varieties that locally looks like the embedding of the open torus into a [toric variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toric_variety).
torsion of a [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve) measures how sharply it is twisting out of the [osculating plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osculating_plane).
torsor or a principal bundle is an analogue of a [principal bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_bundle) in [algebraic topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_topology).

torus action on an [algebraic variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_variety) is a [group action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group-scheme_action) of an [algebraic torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_torus) on the variety.

torus bundle, in the sub-field of [geometric topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_topology) in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), is a kind of [surface bundle over the circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_bundle_over_the_circle), which in turn is a class of [three-manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-manifold)s.

total absolute curvature of a [smooth curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_curve) is a number defined by integrating the [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value) of the [curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature) around the curve.

total-boundedness is a generalization of [compactness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) for circumstances in which a set is not necessarily [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_(topology)).
track gauge is the distance between the two rails of a [railway track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_track).

transition curve (also, spiral easement or, simply, spiral) is a spiral-shaped length of highway or [railroad track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_(rail_transport)) that is used between sections having different profiles and radii, such as between straightaways ([tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangent)s) and curves, or between two different curves.

tractor bundle is a particular [vector bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_bundle) constructed on a [conformal manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_manifold) whose fibres form an [effective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) [representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_representation) of the [conformal group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_group) (see [associated bundle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_bundle)).

trajectoid is a geometric shape designed to trace a predetermined general periodic trajectory on the plane.

two-dimensional flow is a form of [fluid flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_flow) where the [flow velocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow_velocity) at every point is parallel to a fixed plane.

two-dimensional liquid (2D liquid) is a collection of objects constrained to move in a [planar space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planar_space) or other [two-dimensional space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-dimensional_space) in a [liquid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid) state.

two-dimensional space is a [mathematical space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_space) with two [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension)s, meaning [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) have two [degrees of freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degrees_of_freedom): their locations can be [locally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_property) described with two [coordinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate)s or they can move in two independent directions.

Two-point tensors, or double vectors, are [tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor)-like quantities which transform as [Euclidean vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector)s with respect to each of their indices.

Ubersketch is a moniker for a collection of sketches created in [The Geometer's Sketchpad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Geometer's_Sketchpad) by the PRISM-NEO project which mimic ([virtual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_manipulatives_for_mathematics)) [manipulatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manipulative_(mathematics_education)), such as the ones found at The National Library of Virtual Manipulatives.
Ubuntu Titling or Ubuntu-Title is a rounded geometric sans-serif font.

Uhlenbeck's compactness theorem is a result about [sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence) of (weak Yang–Mills) connections with uniformly bounded [curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curvature_form) having weakly or [uniformly convergent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_convergence) subsequences up to [gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory).

Uhlenbeck's singularity theorem is a result allowing the removal of a [singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_(mathematics)) of a [four-dimensional Yang–Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-dimensional_Yang–Mills_theory) field with finite energy using gauge.

Ulam's packing conjecture, named for [Stanisław Ulam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanisław_Ulam), is a [conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) about the [highest possible packing density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_problem) of identical [convex solids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_set) in three-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space).

Veiling glare is an imperfection of performance in [optical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optics) instruments (such as [cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameras) and [telescopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telescopes)) arising from incoming [light that strays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stray_light) from the normal image-forming paths, and reaches the focal plane.
Vercetti Regular, also known as Vercetti, is a single-weight [sans serif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sans_serif) [font](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Font).

Vermeil's theorem essentially states that the [scalar curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_curvature) is the only (non-trivial) absolute invariant among those of prescribed type suitable for [Albert Einstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein)’s theory of [General Relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Relativity).

Vertical exaggeration (VE) is a [scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scale_(ratio)) that is used in [raised-relief map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raised-relief_map)s, [plans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plans_(drawings)) and [technical drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_drawing)s ([cross section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(geometry)) perspectives), in order to emphasize vertical features, which might be too small to identify relative to the horizontal scale.

vesica piscis is a type of [lens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lens_(geometry)), a mathematical shape formed by the [intersection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_(Euclidean_geometry)) of two [disks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk_(mathematics)) with the same radius, intersecting in such a way that the center of each disk lies on the perimeter of the other.

vicinal (from [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin) vicinus = neighbor), abbreviated vic, is a [descriptor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descriptor_(chemistry)) that identifies two [functional group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_group)s as bonded to two adjacent [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon) atoms (i.e., in a 1,2-relationship).
Vietoris–Rips complex, also called the Vietoris complex or Rips complex, is a way of forming a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) from distances in a set of points.

definition: Vinberg's algorithm is an algorithm, introduced by [Ernest Borisovich Vinberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Borisovich_Vinberg), for finding a [fundamental domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_domain) of a [hyperbolic reflection group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_reflection_group).

Virasoro conjecture states that a certain [generating function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_function) encoding [Gromov–Witten invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gromov–Witten_invariant)s of a [smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_point_of_an_algebraic_variety) [projective variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_variety) is fixed by an action of half of the [Virasoro algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virasoro_algebra).
visibility graph analysis (VGA) is a method of analysing the inter-visibility connections within buildings or urban networks.

Visual calculus, invented by [Mamikon Mnatsakanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamikon_Mnatsakanian) (known as Mamikon), is an approach to solving a variety of [integral calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral) problems.

Visvalingam–Whyatt algorithm, or simply the Visvalingam algorithm, is an algorithm that [decimates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimation_(signal_processing)) a curve composed of line segments to a similar curve with fewer points, primarily for usage in [cartographic generalisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartographic_generalisation).

Viviani's curve, also known as Viviani's window, is a [figure-eight-shaped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemniscate) space [curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve) named after the Italian mathematician [Vincenzo Viviani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincenzo_Viviani).

volume entropy is an asymptotic [invariant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_(mathematics)) of a [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold) that measures the exponential growth rate of the volume of [metric ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_ball)s in its [universal cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_cover).

volume form or top-dimensional form is a [differential form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_form) of degree equal to the [differentiable manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiable_manifold) dimension.

von Neumann conjecture stated that a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) G is non-[amenable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenable_group) [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) G contains a [subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgroup) that is a [free group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_group) on two [generators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generating_set_of_a_group).
von Staudt conic is the point set defined by all the absolute points of a polarity that has absolute points.
Voronoi diagram is a [partition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_a_set) of a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) into regions close to each of a given set of objects.
